policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will safeguard up to $500 in cash and $500 in personal effects for a resident only by mutual consent, and will give each such resident a verified statement at least every 3 months (s. 429.27(3)-(4), F.S.). If the facility acts under a power of attorney for a resident, it will keep a copy of the monthly written statement of every transaction made for that resident. If the facility maintains a separate trust fund, it will keep a copy of the quarterly statement of funds and property disbursed (Rule 59A-36.015(3)(j)-(k), F.A.C.). The facility will carry a surety bond if it is representative payee or holds a power of attorney for any resident (s. 429.27(2), F.S.; Rule 59A-36.013(3), F.A.C.). Resident funds will not be co-mingled with facility funds. A single trust account is allowed only if a separate written accounting is kept for each resident (Rule 59A-36.013(2)). Staff will not borrow from, accept gifts from, or use the money or property of any resident.

definitions.definition: Money held by the facility for residents, kept separate from facility operating funds, with a separate written accounting for each resident.
A person or organization appointed to receive and manage a resident's government benefits on the resident's behalf.
A legal document that authorizes someone to act for the resident in financial or other matters.
A written accounting of the resident's funds and property held, reviewed and confirmed by the facility and given to the resident or representative.
A bond that protects the resident's funds from loss and is required when the facility is representative payee or holds a power of attorney.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) will decide whether the facility will hold resident funds, serve as representative payee, or act under a power of attorney. If it will do any of these, the Administrator will purchase the surety bond before the facility takes on that role (see GOV-06).
The facility will not hold a resident's cash or personal effects unless the resident or representative agrees. The agreement will be in writing, signed and dated, and will list what is being held.

Safekeeping for any one resident is limited to $500 in cash and $500 in personal effects. If a resident wants the facility to hold more, the Administrator will explain the limit and suggest other options, such as a bank account managed by the resident or representative.

When taking cash or valuables, two staff members (the staff member and a second employee or the Administrator) will count or inventory them in the resident's presence. Both employees and the resident or representative will sign the receipt, and the resident gets a copy.
Funds will be stored in a locked safe or locked cabinet, with access limited to the Administrator and one designated staff member. The Administrator will keep a list of those authorized.

Each deposit and withdrawal will be written on the resident's individual ledger on the day it occurs. It will show the date, amount, purpose, the staff member's signature and the signature of the resident or representative.

If a trust account is used, it will be a separate account from facility operating funds. A single trust account may hold funds of more than one resident only if the business office keeps a separate written accounting for each resident.

The business office will never deposit resident funds into a facility operating account or pay facility expenses from resident funds. The Administrator will reconcile the trust account to the individual ledgers monthly and sign the reconciliation.

At least every 3 months the business office will prepare a verified statement for each resident whose cash or personal effects are held. The Administrator will review it and give it to the resident or representative, who will sign a receipt. The facility will keep a copy.

If the facility acts under a power of attorney for a resident, the business office will prepare a monthly written statement of every transaction made for that resident, give it to the resident or the person the document designates, and keep a copy.
If the facility maintains a separate trust fund, the business office will prepare a quarterly statement of the funds and property disbursed, and keep a copy.

Staff will not accept loans or gifts from residents, will not witness or sign legal or financial documents for residents on their own behalf, and will not use a resident's property or money for any personal purpose.

When a resident leaves or dies, the business office will give an itemized final accounting. Funds and property will be returned to the resident or the legally authorized person, and a signed receipt will be kept (see HCS-09 and ADM-05).

Staff will report any missing money or property to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator will investigate, notify the resident or representative, and, if theft or exploitation is suspected, report under SAF-01 and record the matter under SAF-02.
The Administrator will review the resident funds records during quarterly quality assurance reviews (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether the facility will hold funds, ensures the surety bond is in force when required, reconciles accounts monthly, and investigates losses.
Keeps individual ledgers and separate accounting, prepares monthly and quarterly statements, and keeps resident funds separate from facility funds.
Do not borrow from, accept gifts from or use resident money or property, and report any missing funds or property immediately.
Agree in writing to any safekeeping arrangement, review statements and report discrepancies.

documentation: Signed safekeeping agreements and receipts for cash and personal effects
Individual resident ledgers showing each transaction
Verified statements issued at least every 3 months, with the resident's signed receipt
Monthly transaction statements for residents under power of attorney
Quarterly statements of funds and property disbursed from any trust fund
Monthly trust account reconciliations signed by the Administrator
Evidence of the surety bond when required
Records of any loss investigation and report

policies.title: Advance Directives and Do Not Resuscitate Orders
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admission staff, nursing and direct care staff, residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To inform residents of their right to make decisions about their health care, to prevent any advance directive or DNRO from being used as a condition of admission, and to make sure an executed Do Not Resuscitate Order is known, available and honored in an emergency.
policies.policy: At admission, [AGENCY NAME] will give each resident or representative Form SCHS-4-2006, "Health Care Advance Directives - The Patient's Right to Decide" (or a substantially similar document under Florida law), and DH Form 1896 (Rule 59A-36.009(1)(a), F.A.C.). The facility will never require a resident to execute or waive DH Form 1896 or any advance directive as a condition of admission or treatment. Doing so could expose the facility's license to enforcement action (Rule 59A-36.009(1)(a), (2)). The facility will document in each resident's record whether a DH Form 1896 has been executed. If one has, the yellow copy will be kept in the record. If a copy was not received, the facility will document that it was requested (Rule 59A-36.009(1)(b)). The executed form will be readily available to medical staff in an emergency (Rule 59A-36.009(1)(c)). Staff trained in CPR, or a health care provider present, may withhold CPR when a valid DH Form 1896 is in place. For a hospice resident, staff will call hospice immediately, and hospice procedures take precedence (Rule 59A-36.009(3)). This policy is part of the admission package (Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)11).

definitions.definition: A written instruction, such as a living will or the designation of a health care surrogate, that states a person's health care wishes or names someone to decide if the person cannot.
A Do Not Resuscitate Order, documented on DH Form 1896, signed by a physician (and the patient or representative), directing that CPR not be started if the person's breathing or heart stops.
The Florida form used for a Do Not Resuscitate Order; the yellow copy is the one that is given to emergency responders.
"Health Care Advance Directives - The Patient's Right to Decide," the information document that explains a person's right to make health care decisions.
A person designated in writing to make health care decisions for a resident who cannot make them.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) will keep a supply of Form SCHS-4-2006 (or a substantially similar document) and blank DH Form 1896 for the admission package, and will confirm the forms are current at each annual policy review (see GOV-03).

At or before admission, the admission staff member will give the resident or representative both documents and explain that they describe the right to accept or refuse treatment and to make an advance directive.

The admission staff member will tell the resident or representative that executing an advance directive or a DNRO is the resident's choice, and that it is not required for admission or treatment. Staff will not ask a resident or representative to sign a waiver of the form.
Admission staff and any other facility staff will not discourage a resident from completing an advance directive or a DNRO, and will not pressure a resident toward either decision.

The admission staff member will ask whether the resident has an executed advance directive, a designated health care surrogate or proxy, a guardian or a power of attorney, and will ask for copies of any such documents.
The staff member will document in the resident's record whether a DH Form 1896 has been executed, with the date of the entry and the staff member's signature.

If a DH Form 1896 has been executed, the staff member will place the yellow copy in the resident's record in the designated, easily found location (the front of the chart or the emergency information folder). If the resident has the form but a copy was not received, the staff member will request a copy and document the request and the date.

The Administrator or designee will make sure the executed DH Form 1896 is readily available to medical and emergency personnel, and will list in the resident's emergency information sheet that a DNRO is in place.

The facility will keep any health care surrogate, proxy, guardian or power of attorney documentation in the resident's record (Rule 59A-36.015(3)(m)). The business office and care staff will know where these documents are kept.
If a resident without an executed DH Form 1896 has a breathing or cardiac emergency, staff trained in CPR will begin CPR and call 911 immediately (see SAF-10 and HCS-04).

If a valid executed DH Form 1896 is in place, staff trained in CPR, or a health care provider present, may withhold CPR. Staff will call 911 or the resident's physician as the situation requires and will present the form to the responding personnel.
If the resident is in hospice, staff will call hospice immediately in a cardiac or respiratory arrest. Hospice procedures take precedence (see HCS-08).

If a resident or representative later asks to execute, change or revoke a DNRO or advance directive, staff will tell the Administrator promptly. The Administrator will contact the resident's physician, update the resident record and emergency information sheet, and inform all shifts the same day.
The resident's DNRO status will be reviewed at each reassessment and each significant change and documented in the record (see ADM-02 and ADM-03).
The facility's DNRO and advance directive policy is included in the admission package and attached to the resident contract (see RR-04).
The Administrator will train all direct care staff on this policy at orientation and annually, including how to find the DH Form 1896 for each resident quickly (see STF-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains forms and this policy, ensures no one is required to execute or waive a DNRO as a condition of admission, and makes sure the form is available in emergencies.
Gives the forms at admission, explains them, asks about existing directives, and documents whether DH Form 1896 is executed.
Know where each resident's DH Form 1896 is kept, follow the policy in an emergency and present the form to responders.
Decide whether to execute a DNRO or advance directive and give the facility copies of any executed documents.

documentation: Record that Form SCHS-4-2006 and DH Form 1896 were given at admission
Documentation in each resident record of whether DH Form 1896 is executed
Yellow copy of any executed DH Form 1896, or note that a copy was requested
Copies of health care surrogate, proxy, guardian or power of attorney documents
Emergency information sheets showing DNRO status
Staff training records on this policy

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, students and contractors of [AGENCY NAME] who create, use, see or hear resident information; all residents and their representatives; all license types (standard, ECC, LNS, LMH).
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and confidentiality of resident information and communications, to make records available to the people entitled to them, and to meet Florida record-keeping and access requirements for assisted living facilities.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps resident records confidential and releases them only to the resident and to others authorized by Rule 59A-36.015, F.A.C., by written authorization, or by law. Residents have the right to private communication, including private use of the telephone (Rule 59A-36.007(5)(f), F.A.C.). Records are kept at the licensed physical address and are available to AHCA during inspections, as Rule 59A-36.015 requires. The facility will decide in writing whether it is a HIPAA covered entity, for example because it bills electronically for health care services. If it is a covered entity, it will follow 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164. If it is not, it will apply this policy as operator best practice and will not claim HIPAA status it does not have.

definitions.definition: All written and electronic records the facility keeps about a resident, including the admission package, health assessment, medication records, the record of significant changes, incident reports and the resident contract.
The resident, the legal representative, designee, surrogate, guardian, attorney in fact or case manager, the resident's estate, and others authorized in writing by the resident or by law.

A health plan, health care clearinghouse or health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with a standard transaction, such as electronic billing, as defined in 45 CFR Part 160.
Individually identifiable health information about a resident, in any form, that the facility holds.

procedures: Within 30 days of licensure and before the first admission, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will review whether the facility conducts any electronic standard transactions (for example electronic billing of health plans or Medicaid) and will decide whether the facility is a HIPAA covered entity.

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will record the decision, the date and the reasons on the HIPAA Status Determination form and keep it with the compliance files. The decision will be re-reviewed annually and whenever billing practices change.

If the facility is a covered entity, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will serve as privacy official. The facility will provide each resident with a Notice of Privacy Practices at admission, obtain an acknowledgment, and follow 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164. If it is not a covered entity, the facility will apply the steps below as best practice.
All staff will complete privacy and confidentiality training during orientation and annually. Staff will sign a confidentiality agreement, which is filed in the personnel record.

Resident records will be stored in locked cabinets or in password-protected electronic systems. Access will be limited to staff who need the information to do their jobs. Charts will not be left open or unattended in common areas.
Staff will discuss resident information only with authorized persons and only in places where other residents and visitors cannot overhear.

When someone requests a record, the staff member on duty will verify the requester's identity and authority before releasing anything. Authority means that the person is on the authorized list in this policy, holds a signed authorization from the resident or representative, or is requesting the record under a legal requirement.

Written authorizations from the resident or representative must be signed and dated, name the person or agency to receive the information and describe what may be released. They are filed in the resident record. A resident or representative may revoke an authorization in writing at any time.

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the designee will make the record available to the resident or representative on request during business hours. The facility will not charge a resident for reviewing the record.

When a resident leaves the facility, the administrator or designee will give the resident a copy of the resident's records, as Rule 59A-36.015(3)(q), F.A.C. requires. The copy will be handed to the resident or representative or sent in a way that protects privacy, and the release will be documented.

Staff will give residents private use of the telephone and will not listen to or monitor calls. Staff will also deliver mail and messages unopened and allow private visits in a private space, consistent with RR-01. Any necessary restriction must be documented and must comply with law.

Records will be kept at the facility's physical address and will be readily available to AHCA surveyors. Resident contracts will be kept for 5 years. Other resident records will be kept for at least 2 years after the resident leaves, as Rule 59A-36.015 requires. They will then be destroyed securely, by shredding or by permanent electronic deletion.
Staff will not photograph or record residents, or post resident information or images on social media, without written consent from the resident or representative.

Any staff member who sees or suspects an improper use or disclosure of resident information will report it to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] the same day. The administrator will investigate within 3 business days, correct the problem, notify the affected resident or representative, and document the outcome. Staff who violate this policy will be disciplined up to and including termination.
Privacy compliance, including training completion and any reported breaches, will be reviewed as part of the quality program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Make and document the HIPAA status decision, act as privacy contact, approve record releases that are not routine, investigate breaches and ensure records are kept and retained as required.
Protect resident information, share it only with authorized people, complete privacy training and report improper disclosures immediately.
Verify authority before release, keep the release log and file authorizations.
Tell the facility whom they authorize to receive information and update authorizations when their wishes change.

documentation: HIPAA Status Determination form with date and annual review
Staff confidentiality agreements and privacy training records
Signed resident authorizations to release information and revocations
Record release log, including copies given at departure
Privacy incident reports and corrective actions
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments, if the facility is a covered entity

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All staff who take part in marketing, inquiries, screening, admission, service delivery, retention and discharge decisions; all applicants and residents.
federal: Title VI, 42 U.S.C. 2000d (if the facility receives federal financial assistance)
policies.purpose: To make sure that admission and retention decisions are based only on the criteria in Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C. and the individual assessment of each person, and that residents who do not read or understand English can understand the facility's policies and their rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate against any applicant or resident on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, disability, familial status, age (other than the age 18 and older admission requirement) or any other basis protected by law. Admission decisions are based on the criteria in Rule 59A-36.006(1), F.A.C. and on the individual assessment of the person's strengths, needs and preferences, and on no other basis. A person with HIV infection may be admitted if otherwise eligible. Admission documents are provided in English, as the rule requires. If a resident cannot read or understand English and translated documents are not available, the facility will explain its policies to a family member, friend or other individual who can communicate them to the resident. The facility will make reasonable modifications for people with disabilities and will follow the ADA. If the facility receives federal financial assistance, it will also comply with Title VI.

definitions.definition: A change to a policy, practice or procedure that lets a person with a disability use the facility's services equally, unless it would fundamentally change the service or impose an undue burden.
A person who does not speak English as a primary language and has a limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English.
A family member, friend or other individual who can explain the facility's policies to a resident in a language or format the resident understands.

procedures: Staff who answer inquiries will give every caller or visitor the same information about services, rates and admission criteria. Staff will not ask or screen about protected characteristics, except age, which must be 18 or older.

During screening, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will apply only the admission criteria in Rule 59A-36.006(1) and the facility's written admission policy (ADM-01). The decision will be documented on the screening form with the specific criteria relied upon.

A diagnosis of HIV infection is not a reason to deny admission. The administrator will evaluate an applicant with HIV infection using the same criteria as any other applicant, including the ability to meet the person's needs.

Any decision not to admit a person must be made by the administrator, documented with the specific criteria relied upon, and explained to the applicant or representative. It will be reviewed for consistency with this policy.
At first contact, staff will ask whether the applicant or representative needs language assistance or an accommodation for hearing, vision, speech or cognitive impairment, and will record the answer.

Required admission documents are provided in English. If the applicant cannot read or understand English, the admissions staff member will check whether translated versions are available and provide them if they are.

If translated documents are not available, the admissions staff member will arrange for a family member, friend or other individual chosen by the resident to explain the facility's policies, including the contract, rates, house rules, the Bill of Rights, the grievance process and the DNRO policy. The facility may also use a qualified interpreter. The facility will not rely on another resident for this purpose.

The staff member will document the name and relationship of the communicator, the language used, the date, and the items explained. The communicator and the resident or representative will sign the explanation record where possible.

Staff will provide reasonable modifications on request, including accessible rooms, larger-print documents, reading documents aloud, or extra time to review them. Requests and responses will be recorded in the resident record.

The administrator will post and distribute the Bill of Rights and complaint information as required (RR-01, RR-02) and will make sure residents with limited English proficiency are told how to file a grievance.

Staff will not treat residents differently in room assignment, meals, activities, visiting or care because of a protected characteristic. Residents are not required to take part in religious services or activities.

A resident or applicant who believes they have been discriminated against may file a grievance under RR-02. The administrator will investigate within the time frames in that policy and will take corrective action when discrimination is found.
Staff will receive training on this policy at orientation and annually. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will review admission denials and language assistance records at least annually as part of GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Make or approve all admission decisions on permitted criteria only, arrange language access and accommodations, and review denials and complaints.
Ask about language and accommodation needs, provide English documents and arrange explanations of policies, and document them.
Treat all residents and applicants equally and report discrimination concerns to the administrator.

documentation: Screening and admission decision forms listing the criteria relied upon
Record of language or accommodation needs and requests
Record of the explanation of policies to a family member, friend or other communicator, with name, date and items covered
Accommodation requests and the facility's responses
Grievances alleging discrimination and their resolution
Staff training attendance records

policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admissions staff, nursing staff and any staff who take part in inquiries, screening, admission and the admission package; all prospective residents.
policies.purpose: To admit only people whom the facility is licensed and able to serve, to obtain the medical exam and admission documents Florida requires, and to give each resident the required information before or at admission.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits a person only after the administrator determines that the person meets the admission criteria in Rule 59A-36.006(1)(a), F.A.C., that the facility can meet the person's needs, and that the required medical exam and documents are in order. The decision is based on the assessment of the person's strengths, needs and preferences, the medical exam, the admission policy and services offered, and the facility's ability to meet the fire safety standards of chapter 69A-40, F.A.C. A DNRO or advance directive is never required as a condition of admission.

definitions.definition: The AHCA Resident Health Assessment form (April 2021 edition) or the health care practitioner's own form, used to document the face-to-face medical exam required for admission.

The written materials describing admission criteria, rates, services, house rules, the DNRO and advance directive policy, ECC criteria if applicable, a description of any ADRD program if advertised, and elopement policies.
A licensed professional authorized by Florida law to perform the face-to-face medical exam of a resident.
Comprehensive Assessment and Review for Long-Term Care Services, the Department of Elder Affairs screening whose assessment may substitute for the medical exam.

procedures: Admissions staff will complete a pre-admission screening with the applicant and representative, covering diagnoses, medications, ADL needs, mobility and transfers, behavior, dietary needs, cognitive status, mental health history and the applicant's preferences. The results are recorded on the pre-admission screening form.

The administrator will compare the screening results with the Rule 59A-36.006(1)(a) criteria. Admission may proceed only if the person is 18 or older; is free of communicable disease likely to be transmitted to others; can perform ADLs with supervision or assistance; can transfer (assistance of more than one person is permitted); can take medication by self-administration, assistance or administration; has dietary needs the facility can meet; is not a danger to self or others; does not need 24-hour licensed mental health treatment; is not bedridden, unless receiving hospice; has no stage 3 or 4 pressure sores; does not need 24-hour nursing supervision; and does not need skilled rehabilitative services.

The administrator will check the applicant's needs against the excluded nursing services. For standard, LNS and LMH licenses, these are an artificial airway (CPAP and BiPAP are permitted), tube feeding assistance, blood gas monitoring, post-surgical drains or wound vacuums, blood products, and unstabilized surgical wounds. Facilities with a standard license or an LMH-only license also exclude dialysis and IV therapy performed in the facility. The facility will not admit an applicant who needs an excluded service.

If [AGENCY NAME] holds an ECC license, applicants who need services under the ECC program will be screened under HCS-11 and the ECC admission criteria, and the ECC disclosure will be given before admission.

The administrator will confirm that the facility can meet the applicant's needs with its license type, staffing and services, and that the facility can meet the chapter 69A-40 fire safety standards for the person's evacuation ability. If the facility cannot meet the needs, the administrator will tell the applicant or representative and document the reason (see RR-08 for nondiscrimination).

Before admission, admissions staff will obtain the face-to-face medical exam, which must be completed by a health care practitioner within 60 days before or 30 days after admission, on AHCA Form 1823 or the practitioner's form. The exam must state whether the person has any communicable disease and what level of assistance the person needs.

If the exam is incomplete when the person is admitted, the administrator will list the missing items, request them from the practitioner, and document that they were obtained within 30 days of admission. If they are not obtained, the administrator will reassess appropriateness of continued residency.

A CARES assessment may be accepted in place of the exam when it covers the required information. For a resident placed by DCF or another agency, the exam must have been done within 30 days before placement.

A temporary emergency placement by DCF is exempt from the exam for up to 30 days. The facility will log the person in the admission/discharge log, count the person in the census, and will not accept the placement if it would exceed licensed capacity.

Before admission, the facility will make the written admission package available to the applicant or representative. It includes the admission criteria, rates, services provided, house rules, the DNRO and advance directive policy, the ECC criteria if the facility is licensed for ECC, a description of the ADRD program if the facility advertises one, and the facility's elopement policies.

At or before admission, the facility will give the resident or representative a copy of the resident contract (see RR-04), the admission package, the Bill of Rights (RR-01) and the Ombudsman brochure (RR-03), and will have the recipient sign an acknowledgment of receipt.

At admission, the facility will give the resident or representative the DNRO form (Form SCHS-4-2006 or equivalent) and DH Form 1896, explain the DNRO policy, and record in the resident record whether DH Form 1896 has been executed. The facility will not require a DNRO as a condition of admission. See RR-06.

If the facility staff will assist with medication in a way that requires only unlicensed staff, the administrator or a designee will obtain written informed consent from the resident or surrogate before admission or at admission, and will tell the resident the professional qualifications of the staff who will assist. The consent is filed in the resident record.

The administrator will record the admission in the admission/discharge log on the day of admission. Within 30 days of admission, staff will complete the elopement risk assessment and the initial health assessment as required in ADM-02.
The administrator will sign and date the admission decision on the screening form, noting that the criteria were reviewed, and the full admission file will be stored in the resident record (ADM-03).

responsibilities.duty: Make the final decision on appropriateness of placement, confirm criteria and exam, make sure the package and required documents are provided, and maintain the admission/discharge log.
Conduct pre-admission screening, collect and track the medical exam and give the admission package and acknowledgment forms.
Review nursing needs against excluded services and licensed scope before admission.
Complete the face-to-face exam and form.

documentation: Pre-admission screening form with administrator's signed admission decision
AHCA Form 1823 or the practitioner's form, and a log of missing items obtained within 30 days
CARES assessment or DCF placement exam, if used
Signed acknowledgment of receipt of the contract, admission package, Bill of Rights and Ombudsman brochure
Record of DNRO form (SCHS-4-2006 or equivalent) and DH Form 1896 given, and whether DH Form 1896 is executed
Written informed consent for unlicensed assistance with medication and disclosure of staff qualifications
Admission/discharge log entry, including temporary emergency DCF placements

policies.title: Resident Assessment and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nursing staff (including LNS and ECC nurses), care staff, and health care practitioners and providers who assess residents of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To assess each resident at admission and at the intervals Florida requires, to detect and respond to significant changes, and to identify when a resident's needs exceed what the facility's license allows.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assesses each resident on admission. After that, each resident has a face-to-face assessment by a health care practitioner at least every 3 years or after a significant change, whichever comes first (Rules 59A-36.006(4) and 59A-36.018(1)(k), F.A.C.). Each resident is assessed for elopement risk by a health care provider or mental health provider within 30 calendar days of admission. Staff contact the health care provider and the family, guardian, surrogate or case manager when a resident shows a significant change. Facilities with ECC or LNS licenses also complete monthly nursing assessments. When a resident's needs exceed the license, the facility gives written notice so that a transfer can be arranged.

definitions.definition: A sudden or major shift in a resident's behavior or health, such as a serious fall, stroke, hospitalization, new pressure sore, marked decline in ADL ability or cognition, or a major change in the level of assistance or the method of medication administration. The facility will use the definition in the AHCA assisted living rules in effect, and the administrator will keep a copy of that definition with this policy after verifying it against the current rule.
An assessment by a health care provider or mental health provider of whether a resident is likely to leave the facility or its grounds without staff knowledge or supervision.
A documented assessment by the facility's nurse of each ECC or LNS resident's condition and the services being provided.

procedures: On admission, the facility will collect the health assessment documents required by ADM-01 and review them within 3 days. The administrator or nurse will note the resident's ADL needs, supervision needs, medication method, diet, mobility, cognition and behavior in the resident record.

The health care provider or mental health provider will assess each resident for elopement risk within 30 calendar days of admission. If the pre-admission health assessment includes an elopement risk assessment, that assessment satisfies this requirement. The administrator will confirm completion by day 30 and record the result.
Residents identified as at risk of elopement will have the risk reflected in the resident record and addressed in SAF-03. Staff will be told of the risk at shift report.

Every resident will have a face-to-face examination by a health care practitioner at least every 3 years, or sooner after a significant change, whichever comes first. The administrator will keep a tickler list showing the next due date for each resident.

At least 60 days before a resident's 3-year reassessment is due, the administrator will notify the resident or representative so that the exam can be scheduled. The completed exam is filed in the resident record.
Care staff will report any apparent significant change to the administrator or nurse on the same shift. The administrator or nurse will review the change the same day.

On finding a significant change, the administrator or nurse will contact the resident's health care provider and appropriate family member, guardian, surrogate or case manager. The contact, the person spoken to and any instructions are documented in the record. See HCS-04 for urgent changes of condition.

After a significant change, the administrator will arrange a new face-to-face assessment by a health care practitioner. The administrator will then decide whether the resident still meets the continued residency criteria (ADM-04) and whether services or the record need to be updated (ADM-03).

If the facility holds an LNS or ECC license, the facility nurse will complete a nursing assessment of each resident receiving those services every month and will write a progress note. For LNS, nursing services are delivered only on a practitioner's order. The nurse reports concerns to the administrator.
For ECC, the nurse and administrator will also review each ECC resident's service plan quarterly (see HCS-11 and ADM-03).

If an assessment shows that a resident's needs exceed what the facility's license and staffing can provide, the administrator will review the facts with the resident or representative and the health care provider. If the facility cannot meet the needs, the administrator will give the resident or representative written notice that a transfer must be arranged, and will follow ADM-05.

If a resident, representative or the facility disagrees about the appropriateness of placement, the administrator will document the disagreement, request input from the health care practitioner and follow the placement dispute process in ADM-05, including notifying the Ombudsman if requested.
The administrator will review the assessment tickler list monthly and report overdue assessments in the quality program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Make sure assessments are completed on time, decide continued residency, issue written notice when needs exceed the license and keep the tickler list.
Complete monthly nursing assessments and progress notes, and report changes.
Observe and report changes in condition promptly.
Complete face-to-face assessments and elopement risk assessments.

documentation: Admission health assessment and AHCA Form 1823 or the practitioner's form
Elopement risk assessment with date and assessor
Face-to-face reassessment (every 3 years or after significant change)
Reassessment tickler list
Documentation of notification of health care provider and family, guardian, surrogate or case manager after significant changes
Monthly nursing assessments and progress notes (ECC/LNS)
Written notice that a resident's needs exceed the license, with proof of delivery

policies.title: Resident Care Record, Significant Change Documentation and Service Planning
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nursing staff, care staff and medication staff who create or update resident records at [AGENCY NAME]; all residents.
policies.purpose: To keep a complete, current written record for each resident, document significant changes and additional services, and prepare the specific written plans that Florida requires for restraint use, ECC, LMH and hospice residents.
policies.policy: Florida's standard ALF rules do not require a comprehensive written care plan for every resident. They do require a written record, updated as needed, of significant changes, illnesses that result in medical attention, changes in the method of medication administration, and other changes that resulted in additional services (Rules 59A-36.007(1) and 59A-36.015(3), F.A.C.). [AGENCY NAME] maintains that record for every resident. It also prepares the additional written plans required for residents who use a prescribed physical restraint, ECC and LMH residents, and residents receiving hospice services.

definitions.definition: A dated written account in the resident record of significant changes, illnesses resulting in medical attention, changes in the method of medication administration, and other changes that resulted in additional services.
The written plan for an ECC resident describing the services provided, reviewed at least quarterly.
The plan for each LMH resident that describes the support the resident needs in the community, prepared with the mental health provider under the cooperative agreement.
The written plan developed by the hospice and the facility, in consultation with each other, for a hospice resident.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will make sure that each resident has a record, kept at the facility's physical address, that includes the admission documents, the health assessment, medication records, the record of significant changes and the other items listed in ADM-01 and the facility's records checklist.

When a significant change, an illness resulting in medical attention, a change in the method of medication administration, or any other change resulting in additional services occurs, the staff member who identifies it will notify the administrator or nurse that shift.

The administrator or nurse will write an entry in the record of significant changes within 24 hours, stating the date, what changed, who was notified, what action was taken (including any new or increased services) and the staff member's name and signature.

If the change affects the resident's ability to meet continued residency criteria, the administrator will follow ADM-04 and ADM-02, including contacting the health care provider and family or representative.

If a physician prescribes a physical restraint for a resident, the administrator and nurse will prepare a written care plan within 14 days of the prescription and before the restraint is used. The plan is filed in the resident record and followed under SAF-04.

For ECC residents, the nurse and administrator will prepare a written service plan, review it at least quarterly, and update it after significant changes. The review dates and updates are signed and filed (HCS-11).
For each LMH resident, the facility will prepare a community living support plan and hold a cooperative agreement with the mental health provider, and will keep both in the resident record (HCS-12).

For a hospice resident, the facility will participate with the hospice in developing the interdisciplinary care plan. The facility will keep the plan in the record and provide only services within the scope of its license (ADM-04, HCS-08).

A resident with a stage 3 or 4 pressure sore may not be admitted or retained. If a stage 2 sore develops, the administrator will document the conditions of continued residency in the record and follow ADM-04 and HCS-07.

Staff will record each resident's weight at admission and every 6 months for residents who receive assistance with ADLs. A weight need not be taken for a hospice resident if the resident, the representative or the physician requests in writing that weights not be taken. That request is filed in the record.
Entries must be legible, dated and signed. Corrections are made by a single line through the error with the date and initials, and never by erasure. Electronic records must show author and date.
Records are kept confidential (RR-07). Resident contracts are retained for 5 years, and other resident records are retained for at least 2 years after the resident leaves the facility.

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will audit a sample of resident records each quarter for complete, current entries on significant changes and required plans, and will report the findings in the quality program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Make sure records are complete and current, approve plans and audit records quarterly.
Prepare ECC service plans, restraint care plans and nursing progress notes, and coordinate with hospice.
Report changes promptly and document care and medication-method changes accurately.
Take part in the community living support plan and cooperative agreement.

documentation: Record of significant changes with dated, signed entries
Restraint care plan (written within 14 days of prescription and before use)
ECC service plans and quarterly review documentation
LMH community living support plan and cooperative agreement
Hospice interdisciplinary care plan
Stage 2 pressure sore condition documentation
Weight records, and any written request that weights not be taken for a hospice resident
Quarterly record audit reports

policies.title: Continued Residency Criteria and Conditions the Facility Cannot Serve
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nursing staff and care staff of [AGENCY NAME] who observe, assess or make decisions about residents' continued residency; all residents.
policies.purpose: To decide consistently whether a resident may continue to live at the facility, to apply the exceptions Florida allows for bedridden residents, stage 2 pressure sores and terminally ill residents, and to identify conditions the facility cannot serve.
policies.policy: The criteria for continued residency are the same as the admission criteria in ADM-01, except for the exceptions in Rule 59A-36.006(4)(a)-(c), F.A.C. A resident may be bedridden for no more than 7 consecutive days unless receiving licensed hospice services. A resident with a stage 2 pressure sore may stay only if the conditions in this policy are met. A terminally ill resident who no longer meets the criteria may stay only if the hospice conditions in this policy are met. A hospice resident receives from facility staff only services within the scope of the facility's license. Nursing staff do not train or delegate excluded skilled nursing tasks to unlicensed persons (Rule 59A-36.006(1)(c)).

definitions.definition: Confined to bed and unable to get out of it or transfer, as defined in the AHCA rules in effect.
A partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis or dermis, presenting as an abrasion, blister or shallow crater, as classified by a health care practitioner.
A licensed hospice that provides services to a terminally ill resident under an interdisciplinary care plan.
A nursing service that the facility's license does not permit, such as those listed in ADM-01, which nursing staff may not train or delegate to unlicensed persons.

procedures: Staff will continually observe residents and report to the administrator or nurse any sign that a resident may no longer meet the admission criteria, such as a new danger to self or others, new need for 24-hour nursing supervision, a transfer need that has increased, or a communicable disease.

On receiving a report, the administrator will review the resident's condition the same day, contact the health care provider and the resident's family, representative or case manager (ADM-02), and arrange a reassessment by a health care practitioner when the change is significant.

Bedridden residents: when a resident is confined to bed, staff will record the first day in the record. The administrator will track consecutive days. If the resident remains bedridden for more than 7 consecutive days and is not receiving licensed hospice services, the administrator will begin the process for discharge or transfer in ADM-05.

Stage 2 pressure sore: when a stage 2 sore is found, the nurse or care staff will notify the administrator the same day and the health care practitioner will be contacted. The resident may stay if the resident contracts directly with a licensed home health agency or nurse, or the facility holds an LNS license and care follows a practitioner's plan of care.
The administrator will document the stage 2 sore condition in the resident record, including who is providing care, the plan of care and the date found. Skin care follows HCS-07.

If the stage 2 sore shows no improvement within 30 days, as documented by a health care practitioner, the facility will begin discharge under ADM-05. A stage 3 or 4 sore requires discharge or transfer.

Terminally ill residents: if a terminally ill resident no longer meets the continued residency criteria, the resident may stay only if hospice admits the resident and the resident consents; the resident or representative and the facility agree to continued residency; hospice and the facility develop an interdisciplinary care plan; and all of this is documented in the resident file.

Before agreeing to keep a hospice resident, the administrator will confirm with hospice what care the facility staff will provide and which services hospice will provide. Facility staff will provide only services within the scope of the facility's license, and hospice will provide the rest (HCS-08).
Hospice procedures take precedence if the resident has a cardiopulmonary arrest, and facility staff will follow an executed DNRO (RR-06).

Nursing staff, including contracted nurses, will not train or delegate excluded skilled nursing tasks to unlicensed staff. If a resident's condition requires a task that is excluded for the facility's license, the administrator will start the process for transfer.

When the administrator concludes that the facility cannot serve the resident, the administrator will meet with the resident and the representative, explain the reasons and give written notice as required in the resident contract and ADM-05, and help arrange an appropriate placement.
The administrator will document each continued-residency decision in the resident record, including the criteria reviewed, the people consulted and the outcome.
The administrator will review all continued-residency decisions, discharges and hospice retentions quarterly as part of GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Make all continued-residency decisions, track bedridden days and stage 2 sore timelines, coordinate with hospice, give written notice and document decisions.
Assess residents' conditions, never train or delegate excluded tasks, and support the plan of care for a stage 2 sore.
Report changes in condition, bedridden status and skin changes immediately.
Develop the interdisciplinary care plan and provide care within their scope.

documentation: Continued-residency review notes and decisions in the resident record
Daily log of consecutive bedridden days
Stage 2 pressure sore documentation: date found, plan of care, practitioner's 30-day assessment
Hospice admission, resident or representative consent, facility agreement and interdisciplinary care plan
Written notices of transfer or discharge with proof of delivery
Quarterly review of retention decisions

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice
policies.applies_to: Administrator, managers, nursing staff, business office and all staff who document resident moves; all residents under the standard license and the ECC, LNS and LMH specialty licenses
policies.purpose: To ensure that every resident discharge, transfer or relocation at [AGENCY NAME] is planned, communicated in writing, documented in the admission/discharge log, and completed with the resident's medications and records handled as Florida rules require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will discharge or transfer a resident only for reasons stated in the resident contract and permitted by Chapter 429, F.S. and Rule Chapter 59A-36, F.A.C. When the administrator or the resident's health care provider decides that the resident needs services beyond those the facility's license allows, the facility will give written notice to the resident, the resident's representative or the acting agency that the resident must arrange transfer. Where the resident has no representative, the facility will refer the resident to the appropriate social service agency. If the parties disagree about whether the placement is appropriate, the process in s. 429.26(8), F.S. applies. The facility will state the notice period required by Florida law and the resident contract, and the administrator will confirm it before any involuntary relocation notice is issued. The facility will notify the family, guardian, health care surrogate or case manager when a resident is discharged or moves out. It will return all medications and give the resident a copy of their records on departure.

definitions.definition: The resident's permanent departure from the facility. It is recorded in the admission/discharge log with the date, reason and the facility or home address of discharge.

A period during which the facility holds the resident's bed under the written bed hold policy in the resident contract, for example during a hospital stay. A discharge is not required while a bed is held.
The person or agency (family member, guardian, health care surrogate, case manager) authorized to act or receive notice for the resident.
Medication left at the facility after the resident departs, once notice has been given and the 15-day waiting period has passed without the medication being claimed.

procedures: The administrator, or the resident's health care provider, identifies in writing that a resident needs services beyond the facility's license or no longer meets continued residency criteria, and records the reasons in the resident care record the same day.

The administrator reviews the resident contract provisions on transfer notice and the bed hold policy, and confirms the notice period required by Florida law and the contract before any involuntary notice is issued. The administrator documents this confirmation.

The administrator meets or speaks with the resident and the representative, family, guardian, health care surrogate or case manager to explain the concern and the options. The staff member documents the discussion in the care record, with date, time and participants.

The administrator issues written notice to the resident, the representative or the acting agency that the resident must arrange transfer. The notice states the reason and the date by which the resident must move. A copy goes in the resident record, and delivery is documented (method, date, person receiving).

If the resident has no representative, the administrator refers the resident to the appropriate social service agency within one business day of giving notice and documents the referral, the agency contacted and the contact name.

If the resident, representative or provider disagrees that the placement is inappropriate, the administrator tells them in writing that the procedure in s. 429.26(8), F.S. applies. The administrator follows that process and keeps all related correspondence in the record.

The nurse or designated staff member assists the receiving provider or home with a transition summary. It includes the current medication list, diagnoses, allergies, diet, DNRO status (if any) and the most recent assessment. Staff document what was sent and to whom.
On the day of a planned discharge, staff notify the family, guardian, health care surrogate or case manager of the move-out date and destination, and document the notification.

Before the resident leaves, the nurse or medication-trained staff member reconciles all medications and returns them to the resident, family or guardian. The person receiving them signs and dates a medication release record that lists each item.
Staff provide the resident or representative with a copy of the resident's records on departure and record in the file what was released, the date and the recipient.

The designated staff member enters the discharge in the admission/discharge log the same day, recording the date of discharge, the reason and the facility or home address of discharge. If a bed is held, the resident is not discharged. A later return after an actual discharge is entered as a new admission entry.

For any medication not collected, staff give written notice to the resident, representative or guardian that it remains at the facility. If it is not claimed after 15 days, the administrator or designee treats it as abandoned and documents the date of the determination.

The administrator or designee disposes of abandoned medication within 30 days of that determination. Disposal is by a pharmacist or by destruction by the administrator or designee with one witness. Both people sign and date the disposal record, which is placed in the resident record.
The business office issues the final accounting and any refund owed under the resident contract and refund policy, and returns the resident's funds and personal property per RR-05.
The administrator reviews each discharge within 7 days to confirm that all documentation is complete and to identify trends for the QA program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on and confirms the basis for discharge, confirms the required notice period, issues written notices, handles referrals and disagreements, and verifies the discharge file is complete.
Documents the clinical basis for the need for services beyond the license, prepares the transition summary and reconciles medications at departure.
Maintains the admission/discharge log, provides copies of records, and files notices and release forms.
Completes the final accounting and refunds per the contract.
Report indications that a resident's needs may exceed what the facility can provide, and do not discuss discharge decisions with unauthorized persons.

documentation: Written notice(s) to the resident, representative or acting agency with proof of delivery
Documentation of the administrator's or provider's determination in the resident care record
Social service agency referral record, where applicable
Admission/discharge log entry (date, reason, address of discharge)
Notification record to family, guardian, health care surrogate or case manager
Medication release record and abandoned medication notice and disposal record (with witness signature)
Record of copy of resident records provided on departure
Final accounting and refund record

policies.title: Medication Management, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nurses, medication-trained staff and all staff who handle, store or dispose of resident medications
policies.purpose: To ensure that medications at [AGENCY NAME] are stored securely, labeled and ordered correctly, kept in accordance with each resident's right to self-administer, and disposed of within the timelines in Rule 59A-36.008, F.A.C.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will encourage and allow residents who are able to self-administer their medications to do so. Residents may keep medications on or off the premises. Medications may be kept in the resident's room only if the room is locked when the resident is absent or the medication is out of sight in a secure place. The facility will use central storage whenever Rule 59A-36.008 requires it. Centrally stored medications will be locked at all times, protected from dampness and abnormal temperature, and kept separate from other residents' medications. Medications will be labeled and ordered as the rule requires, and any discontinued, abandoned or expired medication will be handled and disposed of within the required timelines and documented in the resident record.

definitions.definition: A resident's taking of their own medication without hands-on administration by staff.
Storage of a resident's medication by the facility in a locked area, container or refrigerator under the facility's control.
Over-the-counter medication purchased by the facility for use by residents with a practitioner's order, kept locked and labeled as stock supply.
The daily record of each dose given or assisted, kept for each resident who receives assistance with self-administration or administration.
Unexpired medication that the resident's provider has stopped.
Medication left after a resident's departure and unclaimed after notice and a 15-day wait, or medication that is expired and no longer to be used.

procedures: At admission and whenever medication routines change, the nurse or administrator asks each resident whether they wish to self-administer, and the provider's assessment (ADM-02) is used to determine ability. Residents able to self-administer are encouraged and allowed to do so. The outcome is documented in the care record.

The administrator or nurse decides whether central storage is mandatory for each resident. It is mandatory if the facility administers the medication, the resident asks for it, the provider documents the medication as hazardous, the resident cannot keep it safe, other residents are at risk, or facility rules require it. The decision and reason are documented.

Residents who keep medication in their room are checked at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., weekly] to confirm that the room is locked when they are absent or that the medication is out of sight in a secure place. If either condition fails, central storage is arranged and the resident is informed.

Staff store centrally held medications in a locked cabinet, room, container or refrigerator. Refrigerated medications are in a locked container, locked refrigerator or a locked room. Each resident's medication is kept separate from every other resident's.

The administrator assigns a key or code holder on every shift. Keys or codes must always be accessible to responsible staff on duty and are never left unattended or given to unauthorized persons. The administrator keeps a written list of key and code holders.

The designated staff member checks storage areas [FREQUENCY, e.g., daily] for dampness and abnormal temperature, and for refrigerated medications records the refrigerator temperature. Problems are reported to the administrator the same day.

Staff accept only medication that is correctly labeled and supported by a provider's order. Only a pharmacist may transfer medication from one container to another (pill organizers are the only exception). Staff must not relabel or repackage medication.

When an order reads "as needed" or "as directed," the nurse or trained staff member obtains clarification from the provider and documents it in the record. When directions change, the facility obtains a signed order. A telephone order taken by a nurse is documented immediately, and a written order is obtained within 10 working days.

Sample medications are kept in the manufacturer's packaging or in a container with a label showing the practitioner, resident, date, drug, strength, directions and expiration date. Staff do not use samples that lack this information.

The facility keeps over-the-counter stock supply locked, each item labeled with its name, purchase date and a notice that it is stock supply. Each dose is recorded in the resident's medication observation record under a provider's order.
When a provider discontinues a medication that has not expired, staff either return it to the resident or store it separately in an area marked "discontinued medication."

Within 30 days of determining a medication is abandoned or expired, the administrator or designee disposes of it, either through a pharmacist or by destroying it with one witness. Both sign a disposal record listing the resident, drug, strength, quantity and date. The record is filed in the resident record.

If facility staff perform laboratory tests such as blood glucose, the administrator ensures the facility holds a current CLIA certificate before testing begins. A certificate is not required when residents test themselves or staff only assist using the residents' own equipment. Questions go to the AHCA Laboratory Unit at (850) 412-4500.
The nurse or administrator audits medication storage, labeling, orders and observation records at least monthly and reports results to the QA committee (GOV-04). Corrective actions are documented.
Medication records are kept at the facility's physical address and available for AHCA inspection.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures storage meets rule requirements, assigns key holders, approves disposal and ensures CLIA coverage if testing is done.
Reviews orders and labels, obtains clarification and written orders, determines central storage need, and audits records.
Store, secure and record medications per this policy and report problems immediately.
Observes destruction of abandoned or expired medication and signs the disposal record.

documentation: Resident self-administration and central storage determination
Medication observation records
Provider orders, including signed orders and written follow-up to telephone orders
Storage temperature and inspection logs
Disposal records with witness signature and date of determination
Key and code holder list
CLIA certificate (if applicable)
Monthly medication audit results

policies.title: Medication Administration and Staff Authorization
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nurses, unlicensed staff who assist with self-administration, and all staff who document medication assistance
policies.purpose: To define who at [AGENCY NAME] may assist with or administer medications, the training they must complete, and how doses, refusals and errors are documented.
policies.policy: Only staff who meet the requirements of Rules 59A-36.008 and 59A-36.011, F.A.C. will assist residents with self-administration or administer medications. Unlicensed staff must be at least 18 years old and complete the required 6-hour training before assuming this duty. They may orally advise and verbally prompt residents and observe them take their medications. They may not use judgment or discretion, which includes interpreting vital signs or evaluating or assessing a resident's condition, and they may not fill or manage pill organizers. Administration requires a licensed staff member. The facility will tell residents the professional qualifications of the staff who assist them and will obtain written informed consent when unlicensed staff assist.

definitions.definition: Orally advising the resident of the medication name and dosage and verbally prompting the resident while observing the resident take the medication.
Giving a medication to a resident by a licensed staff member per the provider's order or label.
Interpreting vital signs and evaluating or assessing a resident's condition. Unlicensed staff may not perform these tasks.
The daily record updated at each dose for each resident who receives assistance or administration.

procedures: Before assigning medication duties, the administrator verifies that the staff member is at least 18 years old and has a certificate for the 6-hour medication assistance course taught by a registered nurse or licensed pharmacist, including an in-person demonstration. The administrator places a copy in the personnel file.
New staff do not assist with medications until the certificate is on file. The administrator keeps a current list of staff authorized to assist and a list of licensed staff who administer.

Each authorized staff member completes 2 hours of annual continuing education on medication assistance, which may be online. The administrator tracks due dates and removes the authorization of any staff member whose CE is overdue until it is complete.

At admission and when a resident's needs change, the nurse or administrator tells the resident or representative the professional qualifications of the staff who will assist and obtains written informed consent where unlicensed staff will assist. The consent goes in the resident record.

Before each dose, the assisting staff member checks the resident's medication observation record against the label or order, orally advises the resident of the medication name and dosage, and verbally prompts the resident to take it.
The staff member observes the resident take the medication and immediately records the dose on the medication observation record.

When a resident refuses or misses a dose, or a medication error is found, the staff member records it on the medication observation record, notifies the nurse or administrator immediately, and the provider is informed. Concerns or suspected noncompliance are reported to the provider and documented.

Unlicensed staff do not interpret vital signs, assess a resident's condition, adjust doses, or decide whether to give an as-needed medication. They obtain a licensed staff member's direction or the provider's instruction.
Only a nurse fills pill organizers, and only for residents who self-administer. Unlicensed staff do not fill, refill or manage pill organizers.

When the facility administers medications, a licensed staff member is available to administer per the provider's order or label. The administrator schedules licensed coverage so that all scheduled doses can be given.
When a resident has an unusual reaction or a significant change, the licensed staff member documents it and reports it immediately to the provider, and notifies the administrator.

The medication observation record for each resident shows the resident's name, allergies, provider's name and telephone number, drug, strength and directions, and each dose with any missed dose, refusal or error. It is updated at each dose.
For any medication that functions as a chemical restraint, the nurse keeps a record of the prescribing physician's annual evaluation in the resident record (see SAF-04).
The nurse or administrator reviews medication observation records at least monthly for gaps and errors, retrains staff as needed and reports results to the QA committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Verifies age and training before authorizing staff, tracks annual CE, maintains authorized staff lists, and ensures licensed coverage.
Administers medications, fills pill organizers for self-administering residents, supervises assistance, trains and monitors, reports to providers.
Prompt, observe and document within the limits of this policy; report concerns immediately.
Provides the 6-hour course with in-person demonstration and issues certificates.

documentation: 6-hour course certificates and annual CE records in personnel files
List of staff authorized to assist and to administer
Written informed consent for assistance by unlicensed staff
Daily medication observation records
Reports of refusals, missed doses, errors and unusual reactions, and provider notification
Record of physician's annual evaluation for chemical restraint medications
Monthly medication record review results

policies.title: Nursing Services, LNS License and Limits on Delegation
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nurses (employed or contracted), and all staff who deliver or request nursing-level services; standard license and LNS specialty license
policies.purpose: To state when [AGENCY NAME] must have a nurse, what nursing services it may provide under its license, and what tasks may not be delegated to unlicensed staff.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will have a nurse on staff or under contract whenever Florida rules require nursing services. Under the standard license, this includes assistance with portable oxygen, routine colostomy care of the stoma site and flange placement (or training the resident to do it), and administration of medications. Nursing staff will not train unlicensed persons to perform skilled nursing services and will not delegate the excluded tasks to certified nursing assistants or unlicensed persons. A resident may contract independently with a licensed third party for services if the facility agrees. If the facility holds a Limited Nursing Services (LNS) license under s. 429.07, F.S., it will employ or contract a nurse who is available as needed, provide LNS only on a practitioner's order, and keep monthly nursing assessments and nursing progress notes under Rule 59A-36.022, F.A.C. Staff who provide services requiring licensure must be appropriately licensed or certified, with copies in the personnel file.

definitions.definition: A person licensed in Florida as a registered nurse or licensed practical nurse who is employed or contracted by the facility.
Nursing services the facility is authorized to provide under a specialty LNS license issued by AHCA.
Assigning a task to another person to perform. Excluded nursing tasks may not be delegated to unlicensed staff.
A dated, signed note by the nurse documenting nursing services provided and the resident's response.

procedures: The administrator determines at licensure and annually whether the facility holds a standard license only or also an LNS license. The license type is posted (GOV-02) and recorded in the facility's service description.

The administrator engages a nurse as an employee or under written contract. The contract or job description states availability and duties, including medication administration, oxygen and colostomy assistance and, if LNS, services under practitioner orders.

The administrator verifies each nurse's Florida license before the nurse begins work and annually thereafter. A copy of the license and any required certification is placed in the personnel file, and the administrator tracks renewals.

When a resident needs assistance with portable oxygen or routine colostomy care, the nurse assesses the resident, provides the assistance or trains the resident to do it, and documents the assessment, services and training in the resident record.

Nursing staff do not train unlicensed persons to perform skilled nursing services and do not delegate the excluded tasks to CNAs or unlicensed persons. If an unlicensed staff member is asked to perform such a task, they decline and tell the administrator.

If a resident wants skilled services the facility does not provide, the administrator tells the resident and representative that the resident may contract independently with a licensed third party if the facility agrees. The administrator documents the discussion and the agreement and follows HCS-08 for coordination.
For LNS services, the nurse obtains a practitioner's order before the service is begun. The order is filed in the resident record, and the nurse documents services as ordered.
For LNS residents, the nurse completes a nursing assessment at least monthly and writes nursing progress notes. The nurse signs and dates each and files them in the resident record.
A nurse who takes a telephone medication order documents it promptly and ensures a written order is obtained within 10 working days.
The nurse is recognized as having completed first aid training for staffing purposes. The administrator still records the nurse's license in the staffing records.
Nurses and other staff observe residents and report changes to the provider and administrator as appropriate to their qualifications (see HCS-04).
The administrator reviews the nursing coverage schedule monthly to make sure a nurse is available as needed and for medication administration, and reports gaps to the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Engages nurses, verifies licensure, ensures LNS requirements are met and prohibits delegation of excluded tasks.
Provides nursing services within license and orders, completes monthly LNS assessments and progress notes, and refuses to delegate excluded tasks.
Do not perform skilled nursing tasks and report requests to do so.
Ensures resources for nursing services consistent with the license type.

documentation: Nurse licenses and renewals in the personnel file
Nurse employment or contract agreement
Practitioner orders for LNS services
Monthly nursing assessments and nursing progress notes
Assessment and training records for oxygen and colostomy care
Telephone order and written order follow-up
Record of resident's independent contract with a licensed third party, if any

policies.title: Change of Condition, Physician Notification and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, nurses, managers and the administrator
policies.purpose: To ensure that significant changes in a resident's condition are recognized, reported to the health care provider and the resident's representative, documented, and that hospital transfers are handled safely.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will contact the resident's health care provider and the family, guardian, health care surrogate or case manager whenever a resident exhibits a significant change. All staff will observe residents, document observations in the resident's record and report to the provider as appropriate to their qualifications. Significant changes, illnesses resulting in medical attention, medication administration changes and added services will be documented in the resident record. Health changes that could be due to medications and any unusual reactions will be reported to the provider. Hospital transfers will follow the resident contract's bed hold terms, and the executed DH Form 1896 (DNRO) will be readily available to medical staff in an emergency. For hospice residents, hospice is called first.

definitions.definition: A change in the resident's physical, mental or functional condition that requires medical attention, a change in services or a reassessment.
The facility's written policy in the resident contract on holding a bed during an absence such as a hospital stay.
The Florida Do Not Resuscitate Order form, which must be executed and readily available to medical staff.
The resident's physician, advanced practice provider or other practitioner authorized to order care.

procedures: Every staff member observes residents during care and rounds, and documents observations in the resident record by the end of their shift. Staff report any change in condition immediately to the nurse or manager on duty.

In an emergency or when a resident appears in danger, staff call 911 first, begin CPR or first aid if trained and appropriate, and then notify the administrator. Staff do not delay emergency care to make notifications.
For a hospice resident, staff call the hospice agency first, at the number on the care plan, and follow its directions (see HCS-08).

For a non-emergency change, the nurse or manager contacts the resident's health care provider the same day, describes the change and relevant vital signs or observations, and documents the date, time, person contacted and instructions.
Staff report to the provider any health change that could be due to medications and any unusual reaction. The licensed staff member documents each contact in the resident record (see HCS-02).

The nurse or manager notifies the family, guardian, health care surrogate or case manager of the significant change at the same time as, or immediately after, the provider contact, and documents the notification.

Staff document the significant change, any illness resulting in medical attention, any change in medication administration and any added services in the resident record. The administrator reviews the entry within one business day and determines whether reassessment is needed (ADM-02, ADM-03).
