Before transfer to a hospital or other facility, staff gather the current medication list, allergies, diagnoses, provider and contact information, and a copy of the executed DH Form 1896 if the resident has one. They give the packet to the transport crew or accompanying person.
Staff keep the executed DH Form 1896 in a known, readily available location and tell the emergency crew where it is.

The administrator tells the resident, family or representative of the facility's bed hold policy under the resident contract. Charges continue until written notice of a change in status, unless the resident cannot give notice and has no representative.
The nurse or manager follows up with the hospital within 24 hours to learn the resident's status and expected discharge, and documents the contact.

On return, the nurse reviews the discharge instructions and new orders with the provider as needed, updates the medication record and care plan, and documents any added services. If the resident now needs services beyond the facility's license, the administrator follows ADM-04 and ADM-05.
The administrator reviews the incident for reporting requirements (SAF-02) and trends for the QA committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Observe, document and report changes immediately.
Contact the provider and family or representative, direct emergency calls and prepare transfer information.
Reviews documentation, explains bed hold and charges, determines reassessment needs and decides on continued residency.
Gives orders and instructions in response to reported changes.

documentation: Resident record observations and significant change entries
Provider and family/representative contact log (date, time, person, instructions)
Medication change and unusual reaction reports
Transfer packet: medication list, DNRO (DH Form 1896) status and contact information
Bed hold notice and charges per resident contract
Hospital follow-up and return documentation

policies.title: Dementia and Memory Care
policies.applies_to: Administrator, managers and all staff who work with residents who have Alzheimer's disease or related disorders (ADRD), particularly in secured areas
policies.purpose: To ensure that residents with ADRD at [AGENCY NAME] receive care from properly trained staff, that special care claims are accurate, and that residents at risk of elopement are protected.
policies.policy: If [AGENCY NAME] advertises special care for Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, or maintains a secured area as defined in the Florida Building Code, it will ensure that its staff receive the ADRD training required under Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C. before and while providing that care. The administrator will confirm the required number of hours against the current text of the rule and the related statute and will keep documentation. The facility will keep copies of all ADRD advertisements, give prospective residents the written description of special services required by Florida statute, identify residents with ADRD and mobility limitations in the emergency plan, and place identification on residents at risk of elopement. The facility will not admit or retain a resident who requires 24-hour licensed mental health treatment or who poses a danger to self or others.

definitions.definition: Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, including other dementias.
A part of the facility with controlled egress built and maintained in accordance with the Florida Building Code for such areas.
A resident's risk of leaving the facility without staff knowledge or supervision in a way that could cause harm.
The document required by Florida statute that describes the special services a facility offers to residents with ADRD, given to prospective residents before admission.

procedures: At licensure and annually, the administrator decides whether the facility will advertise ADRD care or operate a secured area, and documents the decision. If neither, residents who need secured memory care are referred elsewhere under ADM-04.

If the facility advertises ADRD special care or has a secured area, the administrator confirms the required ADRD training content and hours in the current text of Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C. and the related statute, and records the requirements in the training plan.

The administrator schedules ADRD training for all required staff as the rule requires, and tracks completion dates by employee. Staff who have not completed it are not assigned to ADRD care without the supervision permitted by the rule.
The training provider issues a certificate or the facility keeps a signed attendance record. The administrator places copies in the personnel file (STF-06).

The facility keeps a copy of every ADRD advertisement (brochures, website pages, social media, signs) in a file at the facility address. The administrator reviews each advertisement before release to make sure it accurately reflects the services provided.
Before admission, staff give each prospective resident or representative the written description of special services required by Florida statute and document the date given.

During pre-admission screening and assessment (ADM-01, ADM-02), the nurse or administrator determines whether the resident has ADRD, the stage, wandering or elopement history and mobility limits, and records them in the resident record.

The administrator adds residents with ADRD and mobility limitations to the specialized-assistance list in the facility emergency plan (SAF-05), and updates the list at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., monthly] and after each admission or change.

For each resident at risk of elopement, staff place identification on the resident's person with the resident's name and the facility's name, address and telephone number, and check it at least daily. Staff keep a current photograph of the resident on file for use in a missing-resident search (SAF-03).
Staff use person-centered approaches to manage behavior. They do not use restraints, restrictive practices or chemical restraints except as allowed under SAF-04.
If a resident requires 24-hour licensed mental health treatment or poses a danger to self or others, the administrator documents the finding and begins the process in ADM-04 and ADM-05.
The administrator reviews ADRD care, training completion, advertising and elopement incidents at least quarterly with the QA committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Confirms training requirements, schedules and tracks training, controls advertising, provides the written description of services and maintains the emergency list.
Identifies ADRD and elopement risk, assesses behaviors and monitors identification.
Complete ADRD training, check resident identification daily and provide person-centered care.
Ensures resources for training and safe secured areas.

documentation: ADRD training certificates and attendance records in personnel files
Copies of all ADRD advertisements
Dated record that the written description of special services was given to prospective residents
Resident assessments identifying ADRD and elopement risk
Emergency plan list of residents with ADRD and mobility limitations
Daily identification check log and resident photo file
QA review notes

policies.title: Falls Prevention
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, the Administrator, and any manager or nurse involved in resident care
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk of falls and fall-related injury among residents of [AGENCY NAME] through daily observation, supervision, safe equipment, medication side-effect awareness, and prompt documentation and follow-up when a fall or near-fall occurs.
policies.policy: Florida's ALF rules contain no standalone falls standard. [AGENCY NAME] therefore anchors its falls prevention practice to the facility's duties to supervise residents and observe each resident's health, safety and well-being daily (Rule 59A-36.007), to document in writing any illness or change that results in medical attention (Rule 59A-36.007), to report observable health changes, including possible medication side effects, to the resident's health care provider (Rule 59A-36.008), and to maintain enough staff to meet residents' scheduled and unscheduled needs (Rule 59A-36.010). Every fall is documented. A fall that causes injury is also reviewed as an incident under SAF-02. Staff do not restrain residents to prevent falls (see SAF-04).

definitions.definition: An unplanned descent to the floor or other lower surface, with or without injury, whether witnessed or found.
An event in which a resident loses balance or nearly falls and is caught, or catches themselves, without reaching the floor.

Conditions that raise the likelihood of a fall, such as prior falls, unsteady gait, use of an assistive device, vision problems, confusion, urgency or incontinence, low blood pressure, and certain medications.
A change in a resident's condition that is documented in the resident record under ADM-03 and may require reassessment, provider notification, or a change in services.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator or designee asks the resident and representative about prior falls, balance problems, dizziness, use of assistive devices, vision and hearing, and fall-related fears. The answers are recorded in the pre-admission and assessment documents (ADM-01, ADM-02).

The person completing the assessment under ADM-02 identifies each resident's fall risk factors and records the resident's needs for supervision, prompting, toileting assistance and device use in the service plan or care notes (ADM-03).

Direct care staff observe each resident daily for changes in walking, balance, alertness, mood, appetite, continence and new complaints of pain or dizziness. Staff report such changes to the shift supervisor before the end of the shift.

The shift supervisor decides whether the change needs a call to the resident's health care provider, and notifies the provider and the resident's representative under HCS-04. The change is recorded in writing in the resident record whenever it leads to medical attention (ADM-03).

Staff report observable changes that may be medication side effects (drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, unsteadiness, fainting) to the resident's health care provider and document the report. Staff do not change, withhold or adjust a medication on their own (HCS-01, HCS-02).

Staff follow HCS-10 by checking each resident's assistive devices for condition and hazards (loose tips, worn tires, broken brakes, wobbly frames) at least during daily care and reporting needed repairs to the Administrator the same day. A device that is unsafe is removed from use or repaired before further use.

Housekeeping and maintenance staff keep walkways, rooms, bathrooms, dining areas and outdoor paths free of clutter, spills, cords and uneven surfaces. Lighting, including night lighting in hallways and bathrooms, is kept working. Staff report hazards immediately and the Administrator tracks repairs (DL-03).

The Administrator schedules enough staff, including at mealtimes, in the morning and evening care periods, and overnight, to meet residents' scheduled and unscheduled needs, and adjusts assignments when residents' fall risks increase (STF-01).

Staff assist residents who need help with toileting, transfers and walking according to the service plan, and offer assistance and prompting at predictable high-risk times (waking, after meals, before bed).

When a resident falls, the nearest staff member stays with the resident, does not move the resident if injury is suspected, calls the shift supervisor and, if serious injury is suspected, or if the resident is unresponsive, calls 911. Staff trained in first aid and CPR respond (SAF-10).

The shift supervisor or designated staff checks the resident for injury and changes in condition, provides first aid within staff training limits, and notifies the resident's health care provider and representative. Staff follow HCS-04 for any change of condition or hospital transfer.

Staff document each fall or near-fall in the resident record the same shift, including date, time, location, who witnessed it, resident statement, apparent injuries, actions taken, and who was notified.

The shift supervisor completes an incident report for every fall under SAF-02. If a fall causes injury, the Administrator reviews it under SAF-02 to decide whether it must be reported externally and acts as that policy directs.

Within 24 hours of the fall, staff increase observation of the resident, including checks for delayed symptoms such as new pain, swelling, bruising, drowsiness or confusion, as directed by the provider, and document those observations.

Within 3 business days of any fall, the Administrator or designee reviews the circumstances, considers whether footwear, lighting, devices, medications, toileting patterns or staffing contributed, and updates the resident's care notes or service plan. If the fall is a significant change, a reassessment is done under ADM-02.
The Administrator reviews falls monthly for patterns by resident, time of day, location and shift, and reports findings to the quality assurance process (GOV-04).
Falls prevention is covered in orientation and in-service training for all direct care staff, including the safe use of assistive devices and emergency response (STF-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures adequate staffing, safe premises and equipment, timely falls review and trend analysis, and staff training.
Responds to falls, directs first aid and 911 calls, notifies the provider and representative, completes the incident report, and ensures follow-up monitoring.
Observe residents daily, assist and supervise per the service plan, check devices, report changes and possible medication side effects, and document falls and near-falls.
Identify and correct environmental hazards and keep lighting and walkways in safe condition.

responsibilities.role: Licensed Nurse (if on staff or contract)
responsibilities.duty: Advises on fall risk, clinical follow-up and any care that requires licensed personnel within the limits stated in HCS-03.

documentation: Fall risk information in the pre-admission and assessment records
Service plan or care notes with fall-related needs
Daily observation notes and records of changes reported to the provider
Fall/near-fall entries in the resident record
Incident reports (SAF-02)
Records of provider and representative notification
Assistive device condition and repair records (HCS-10)
Monthly falls trend review and QA minutes (GOV-04)
Training records

policies.title: Skin Integrity
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, the Administrator, and nurses or third-party providers who treat residents' skin conditions
policies.purpose: To prevent skin breakdown, identify skin problems early, and make sure that residents with pressure sores, wounds or surgical incisions are admitted and retained only as Florida's ALF rules allow.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or retain a resident with a stage 3 or stage 4 pressure sore. A resident with a stage 2 pressure sore may be admitted or retained only under the conditions in Rule 59A-36.006: the resident contracts directly with a licensed home health agency or a licensed nurse for care, or, if the facility holds a limited nursing services (LNS) license, the facility cares for the resident under a health care practitioner's plan of care; the condition is documented in the resident record and in the admission and discharge logs; and the resident is discharged if the sore does not improve within 30 days as documented by a health care practitioner. Treatment of a surgical incision or wound is allowed only when the wound and the underlying condition are stabilized and a plan of care is in the record. A bedridden resident may stay no more than 7 consecutive days unless the resident is enrolled in hospice. All skin changes are observed, reported and documented.

definitions.definition: Localized damage to skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony area, caused by pressure or friction, staged from 1 to 4 by severity.
Partial-thickness skin loss with a shallow open area or blister, with no slough or deeper tissue involvement.
Full-thickness skin loss (stage 3) or loss with exposed muscle, tendon or bone (stage 4). Residents with these conditions cannot be admitted or retained.
Confined to bed because of an inability to transfer or move without total assistance, as provided in Rule 59A-36.006.
A written plan from a health care practitioner or a licensed home health agency or nurse that describes the treatment and monitoring of a wound or skin condition.

procedures: Before admission, the person completing pre-admission screening (ADM-01) inspects, or obtains the health care practitioner's documentation of, the resident's skin and asks about current or recent pressure sores, wounds and surgical incisions. The finding is recorded, including the stage of any pressure sore.
If the resident has a stage 3 or stage 4 pressure sore, the Administrator declines admission, explains the reason to the resident and representative, and documents the decision.

If the resident has a stage 2 pressure sore, the Administrator confirms before admission that either (a) the resident has a contract with a licensed home health agency or a licensed nurse, or (b) the facility holds an LNS license and a practitioner's plan of care is in hand. If neither applies, the resident is not admitted.

For an accepted resident with a stage 2 sore, the Administrator records the condition on the admission log entry and places the home health or nurse contract, or the practitioner's plan of care, in the resident record.

For a resident with a surgical incision or wound, the Administrator admits or retains the resident only when the practitioner's documentation shows that the wound and underlying condition are stabilized, and a plan of care is in the record.
Direct care staff check the resident's skin during bathing, dressing and incontinence care and report redness, open areas, blisters, bruises, swelling or pain to the shift supervisor the same shift.

Staff reposition or encourage position changes for residents with limited mobility as set out in the service plan, keep skin clean and dry, use pressure-relieving cushions or devices as ordered, and encourage fluids and nutrition per diet orders (DL-01).
The shift supervisor notifies the resident's health care provider and representative of any new skin breakdown under HCS-04 and documents the notification and any instructions in the resident record.

Wound care and dressing changes are performed only by the licensed home health agency, the contracted nurse, or, if the facility holds an LNS license, by facility nursing staff under the practitioner's plan of care. Unlicensed staff do not perform treatments beyond their training and authorization (HCS-03).
The Administrator or designee communicates with the home health agency or nurse treating the wound at least every 30 days and at any significant change, and documents that communication under HCS-08.
Beginning on the date a stage 2 sore is documented, the Administrator tracks the 30-day period and obtains written documentation from a health care practitioner on whether the sore has improved.
If the practitioner documents no improvement within 30 days, the Administrator begins discharge planning under ADM-05 and notifies the resident, representative and provider.
If a stage 2 sore progresses to stage 3 or 4, the Administrator immediately notifies the provider and representative and starts discharge planning under ADM-04 and ADM-05.

If a resident becomes bedridden, the shift supervisor notifies the Administrator the same day. The Administrator documents the date the bedridden status began and tracks consecutive days. The resident may not remain more than 7 consecutive days unless enrolled in hospice, and the Administrator starts relocation planning under ADM-04 and ADM-05 if the condition is expected to continue.
The Administrator records the date a stage 2 sore, or any significant skin change, is first documented in the resident record under ADM-03, and keeps admission and discharge log entries current.
Skin integrity and pressure-sore prevention are included in orientation and in-service training for direct care staff (STF-04).

responsibilities.duty: Applies the admission and retention limits, verifies contracts and plans of care, tracks the 30-day and 7-day limits, keeps the logs, and starts discharge planning when required.
Receives staff reports of skin changes, notifies the provider and representative, and documents the notification.
Check skin during care, perform preventive repositioning and hygiene, and report changes the same shift.

responsibilities.role: Licensed Nurse or Home Health Agency
responsibilities.duty: Assess, stage and treat wounds under the practitioner's plan of care and communicate with the facility.
Provides the plan of care and documents whether a stage 2 sore has improved within 30 days.

documentation: Pre-admission skin findings and sore staging
Admission and discharge log entry noting any stage 2 sore (Rule 59A-36.015)
Home health or nurse contract, or practitioner's plan of care
Practitioner documentation of improvement or no improvement within 30 days
Provider and representative notifications
Third-party communication records (HCS-08)
Record of the dates a resident became bedridden
Discharge planning documents (ADM-05)
Training records

policies.title: Hospice, Home Health and Third-Party Provider Coordination
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, managers, nurses and direct care staff who work with residents receiving hospice, home health or other third-party services
policies.purpose: To allow residents to receive services from hospice, home health agencies, private nurses and outpatient clinics, and to make sure those providers coordinate with [AGENCY NAME] and that communication is documented as Florida rules require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows residents to receive third-party services, including home health, private nurse and outpatient clinic services, as long as the resident meets admission and continued residency criteria. Each third-party provider must coordinate with the facility about the resident's condition and services. [AGENCY NAME] documents communication with each third-party provider at least every 30 days and at any significant change. A resident enrolled in licensed hospice may be admitted and may remain in the facility under Rule 59A-36.006 and s. 429.26, F.S., even if bedridden or needing 24-hour nursing, and hospice procedures take precedence if the resident has a cardiac or pulmonary arrest. A copy of this policy is kept on file.

definitions.definition: A home health agency, private nurse, outpatient clinic, hospice or other outside provider that delivers services to a resident in the facility or arranges services for the resident.
A licensed hospice program providing end-of-life care to a resident under an interdisciplinary care plan.
A change in the resident's condition or services that is recorded in the resident record under ADM-03 and requires communication with the third-party provider.
The hospice's written plan of care for the resident, which is kept in the resident record.

procedures: At admission and whenever a resident starts a new outside service, the Administrator or designee records the provider's name, agency, telephone number, type of service, schedule of visits and the practitioner who ordered it in the resident record.

Before a third-party provider starts services, the Administrator confirms that the resident meets admission and continued residency criteria (ADM-01, ADM-04). Services are allowed if the resident meets those criteria.

The Administrator informs each third-party provider in writing that it must coordinate with the facility about the resident's condition and services, and gives the provider the facility's contact person and telephone number [PHONE].

The Administrator or designee communicates with each third-party provider at least every 30 days and at any significant change in the resident's condition. If the provider treats the resident less often than monthly, communication follows the treatment schedule.
Each communication is documented with the date, the provider's name, the method (visit, call, fax, secure message), who spoke, and the information shared or received.

If the Administrator or designee cannot reach a provider, staff make two attempts on separate days and document the name of the person or office contacted, the method, and the date and time of each attempt.
If the facility assists a resident in arranging third-party services and the effort is unsuccessful or the resident or representative declines, staff document why in the resident record.
Staff share relevant observations (for example, changes in skin, appetite, mobility, mood, or medication effects) with the provider and record what was shared. Staff follow HCS-04 for urgent changes.
Staff keep third-party orders, visit notes and plans of care in the resident record, and follow instructions only within the limits stated in HCS-02 and HCS-03 on staff authorization and delegation.

For a resident enrolled in hospice, the Administrator obtains the hospice election documentation, the interdisciplinary care plan, the hospice contact numbers, and the hospice's instructions on medications, comfort care and emergencies, and places them in the resident record.

The Administrator confirms that the resident's care in the facility can be provided safely with hospice support. Hospice residents may be bedridden and may need 24-hour nursing under s. 429.26, F.S., and Rule 59A-36.006, and do not trigger discharge solely for those reasons.
The Administrator coordinates with the hospice to define who provides which parts of care and how staff will carry out the hospice plan of care, and documents any changes.

If a hospice resident has a cardiac or pulmonary arrest, staff immediately contact hospice and follow hospice procedures, which take precedence under Rule 59A-36.009. Staff also follow any executed DNRO (RR-06).
At the death of a hospice resident, staff notify hospice and follow HCS-09.
If a resident revokes or is discharged from hospice, the Administrator reassesses the resident under ADM-02 and applies the continued residency criteria in ADM-04.
The Administrator reviews third-party communication logs monthly to confirm that the 30-day contacts and attempts were made, and reports gaps to quality assurance (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves third-party services, ensures coordination and 30-day documentation, maintains the policy, and coordinates hospice care.
Communicates with providers, documents each contact or attempt, and files provider orders and plans of care.
Report resident changes to the supervisor and follow the plan of care within the limits of their training and authorization.
Coordinate with the facility on the resident's condition and services and share visit findings and plan changes.
Provides the interdisciplinary care plan and direction in an arrest or at death, and supports staff in carrying out the plan.

documentation: Third-party provider list in the resident record
30-day and significant-change communication log, including documented attempts
Documentation of why arranged services were unsuccessful or declined
Hospice election and interdisciplinary care plan (Rule 59A-36.015)
Provider orders and plans of care
This policy, kept on file (Rule 59A-36.015)
Executed DH Form 1896, if any, and hospice emergency instructions (RR-06)

policies.title: Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff, with the Administrator and the shift supervisor responsible for carrying out the steps
policies.purpose: To make sure that the death of a resident is handled with dignity, that the resident's representative, family and hospice are notified, that records and medications are handled correctly, and that required documentation is kept.
policies.policy: When a resident dies, [AGENCY NAME] responds promptly and respectfully, follows the resident's executed DNRO (DH Form 1896) or, for a hospice resident, hospice procedures, notifies the representative or family and hospice according to the contacts in the resident record, records the date of death on the admission and discharge log, handles the resident's medications as the medication rule requires, and retains records for the periods Florida rules set. Whether the death must also be reported as an adverse incident or to another agency is reviewed under SAF-02.

definitions.definition: The Florida Do Not Resuscitate Order form, printed on yellow paper, that directs health care providers not to attempt resuscitation.
The person or persons identified in the resident record as the resident's contacts, such as a family member, guardian or health care surrogate.
A resident's medication left in the facility after a resident dies or leaves and that has not been claimed.
The facility log in which each resident's admission date and discharge or death date are recorded.

procedures: If staff find a resident who appears to have died or who stops breathing or has no pulse, they check the resident's record at once for an executed DH Form 1896 and for hospice enrollment, and call the shift supervisor.
If the resident has no executed DNRO and is not enrolled in hospice, staff call 911 and begin CPR if trained, following SAF-10, until emergency responders take over.
If the resident has an executed DH Form 1896, staff honor it as directed in RR-06 and Rule 59A-36.009, and give the form to emergency responders if they are called.
If the resident is enrolled in hospice, staff immediately contact hospice, whose procedures take precedence, and follow hospice's instructions (HCS-08).
The shift supervisor notifies the Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] immediately, and notifies the resident's health care provider as the provider or hospice directs.

Staff notify the resident's representative and family, and hospice if applicable, using the contacts recorded in the resident record. The person making the call records the time, the person spoken to and what was said. If no one can be reached, staff keep trying and document each attempt.

Staff protect the resident's privacy and the other residents' sensitivities, close the door, and keep the resident's body and surroundings undisturbed until the physician, hospice, law enforcement or medical examiner, as applicable, gives direction about release of the body. Staff follow the funeral home arrangements recorded in the resident record or given by the representative.
The Administrator informs other residents who may be affected in a sensitive manner and offers support, and notifies staff on following shifts.
The Administrator or designee records the date of death on the admission and discharge log.

The shift supervisor completes a written account of the death in the resident record, including the date and time found, circumstances, actions taken, calls made, who was notified, and when the body was released and to whom.
The Administrator reviews the death under SAF-02 to decide whether it must be reported as an adverse incident or to another agency, and makes any report that policy requires.

Within a time frame agreed with the family and no later than the facility's normal discharge procedures, the Administrator returns the resident's medications to the family or guardian where permitted, documenting what was released and to whom, under HCS-01.

Medications that are not claimed, and any abandoned or expired medications, are disposed of within 30 days with documentation of the date, medications, quantity and the staff who witnessed disposal, as HCS-01 specifies.
The Administrator inventories and returns the resident's personal property and funds to the representative or the estate under RR-05 and documents it with a signed receipt.
The Administrator refunds any prepaid amounts and finalizes the account under RR-04.

The resident record is closed and kept at the facility for 2 years after the date of death. The admission agreement and resident contract are kept for 5 years. Records are readily available at [ADDRESS] for inspection.

responsibilities.duty: Directs the response, notifies representatives where needed, reviews the death for reporting under SAF-02, completes the log, return of property, medications and refunds, and record retention.
Checks for DNRO and hospice status, directs staff, makes notifications, documents the event and secures the resident's belongings.
Call for help, follow the DNRO or hospice instructions, protect privacy and support other residents.
Directs response to an arrest or death of a hospice resident and supports the family.

documentation: Admission and discharge log entry with date of death (Rule 59A-36.015)
Written account of the death in the resident record
Record of notification of the representative, family and hospice
DH Form 1896, if executed, and hospice documents
Medication return and disposal records (Rule 59A-36.008)
Property and funds receipt (RR-05)
Incident report and report-review decision (SAF-02)
Retention schedule: resident records for 2 years after departure; contracts for 5 years

policies.title: Assistive Devices Safety
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, maintenance staff, the Administrator, and residents who use assistive devices
policies.purpose: To make sure residents' assistive devices are safe, clean, in good repair and used correctly, and that staff encourage residents' independence in using them.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is responsible for the safe use of residents' assistive devices. This written policy sets requirements and methods for assessing the physical condition of devices that may injure a resident and for recommending repair or replacement. Each resident's assistive devices are documented in the resident record. Direct care staff who use or help with assistive devices must know how to operate them. Devices must be clean, in good repair and free of hazards. Staff encourage residents to use their devices independently as far as they safely can. Communal devices and reusable medical equipment are cleaned and disinfected before and after each use according to the manufacturer's recommendations. This policy is kept on file.

definitions.definition: Equipment that helps a resident with mobility, communication, hearing, vision or daily activities, such as a cane, walker, wheelchair, hearing aid, glasses, dentures, lift or shower chair.
A device or piece of reusable equipment used by more than one resident, such as a shared wheelchair, transfer aid or blood pressure cuff.
A defect or condition that could injure a resident, such as a loose part, frayed cord, worn brake or sharp edge.

procedures: At admission and at each reassessment, the person completing the assessment under ADM-02 asks the resident and representative which devices the resident uses and records each device in the resident record.
The Administrator or designee notes in the record how the resident uses each device, how much help is needed, and any safety concerns, and carries those into the service plan (ADM-03).

New direct care staff are shown how to operate and safely use the devices used by the residents they care for, such as wheelchairs, walkers, lifts, and shower chairs, as part of orientation, and the training is documented (STF-04).
Staff do not use or help a resident with a device they have not been trained to operate. They ask the shift supervisor for instruction first.

Staff visually check each resident's device for condition and hazards whenever they help with it and at least once a week as a documented check. Checks cover frames, wheels, tires, brakes, seat and footrests, handgrips and tips, straps, cords, batteries, and fit.
Staff report any damaged, worn or unsafe device to the shift supervisor immediately. The supervisor takes the device out of use if it may injure the resident and arranges a safe alternative.

The shift supervisor notifies the Administrator of the problem the same day. The Administrator recommends repair or replacement to the resident or representative and records the recommendation and result. If the device is the resident's personal property, the resident or representative decides on repair or replacement. If the facility owns it, the Administrator arranges repair or replacement.
Maintenance staff or a qualified repair provider carries out repairs. Repair or replacement is documented, with the date and the person who repaired.
Staff keep devices clean, wiping down handgrips, trays, seats and frames as part of routine care and when soiled. Hearing aids, glasses and dentures are cleaned and stored safely when not in use.

Communal devices and reusable medical equipment are cleaned and disinfected before and after each use with products and contact times that follow the manufacturer's recommendations, in line with SAF-08.

Staff keep devices within the resident's reach when safe, keep pathways clear, and lock wheelchair brakes during transfers. They encourage residents to use their devices on their own as safely as possible and do not remove a device for staff convenience.

If a resident does not use a recommended device or uses one unsafely, staff encourage proper use, report it to the shift supervisor, and the Administrator informs the resident, representative and health care provider as appropriate.
If a device malfunctions and a resident is injured, staff provide first aid and follow SAF-02 and HCS-04.
The Administrator reviews device checks and repairs monthly and reports patterns to quality assurance (GOV-04). This policy is reviewed under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, arranges repair or replacement, ensures staff are trained, and reviews device checks.
Know how to operate devices, check and clean them, report hazards, and encourage independent use.
Removes unsafe devices from use, arranges a safe alternative, and notifies the Administrator.
Repair or arrange repair of devices and document the work.
Tell staff about device problems and agree on repair or replacement of personal devices.

documentation: List of each resident's assistive devices in the resident record
Service plan or care notes on device use
Weekly device condition checks
Repair, replacement and removal-from-use records
Cleaning and disinfection records for communal devices (SAF-08)
Staff training records on device operation
This policy, kept on file (Rule 59A-36.015)

policies.title: Extended Congregate Care (ECC) Program
policies.applies_to: Only a facility that holds an Extended Congregate Care license; applies to the Administrator, the ECC supervisor, the nurse, and direct care staff
policies.purpose: To describe how [AGENCY NAME] operates its Extended Congregate Care program in compliance with the ECC license requirements, including nursing oversight, staffing, training, disclosure and service plan reviews, so that residents who need more services can safely age in place.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides ECC services only while it holds a current ECC license from AHCA. The ECC license is a specialty license (s. 429.07, F.S.). An ECC license may be provisional for no more than 6 months for a facility licensed for less than 2 years, followed by an unannounced inspection. The facility has a nurse on staff or under contract, completes a nursing assessment for each ECC resident every month, reviews each ECC resident's service plan every quarter, and keeps adequate awake staff at all hours. The Administrator has the experience required for an ECC license (2 years of qualifying experience, with a bachelor's degree substituting for 1 year). Staff receive the ECC training Florida requires. Prospective residents receive the ECC admission and residency criteria, a description of the added services and their costs, and any limits on where ECC residents may live. ECC licensees also meet the ECC staffing rules in Rule 59A-36.021.

definitions.definition: A specialty license that allows an ALF to provide, directly or through contract, additional nursing and personal services to residents who would otherwise need to move to a nursing facility, so that they can age in place.
The person designated by the Administrator to supervise the ECC program and its staff.
The written plan listing the resident's needs and the services the facility will provide, reviewed at least quarterly for ECC residents.
An assessment by the facility's nurse of the ECC resident's health condition and needs, done monthly.

procedures: Before offering ECC services, the Administrator confirms that the facility holds a current ECC license and posts the license under GOV-02. If the facility holds only a provisional ECC license, the Administrator tracks the 6-month limit and prepares for the unannounced inspection that follows.

The Administrator confirms and documents that he or she meets the ECC experience requirement: 2 years of qualifying experience, or 1 year with a bachelor's degree. The documentation is kept in the personnel record (STF-06).

The Administrator and the designated ECC supervisor complete core training plus 4 hours of initial ECC training before the facility is licensed for ECC or, if hired later, within 3 months of starting employment in a licensed ECC facility. They complete 4 hours of ECC continuing education every 2 years.

Each direct care staff member completes 2 hours of ECC in-service training within 6 months of hire. The Administrator keeps the training dates, topics and sign-in sheets in the personnel record (STF-04, STF-06).
The Administrator engages a nurse as a staff member or under a written contract for ECC services and places the nurse's license verification and contract on file (HCS-03).

Before admitting or retaining a resident who needs ECC services, the Administrator confirms that the resident meets the ECC admission and residency criteria in Rule 59A-36.021 and the facility's general admission criteria in ADM-01 and ADM-04.

Before admission, the Administrator gives each prospective resident and representative the ECC residency criteria, a written description of the additional ECC services and their costs, and any limit on where ECC residents may live in the facility. The resident or representative signs a receipt, and the signed copy is put in the resident record (RR-04).
A resident who moves into ECC from the general program is given the same disclosure in writing before the change in services starts, and the admission agreement is updated (RR-04).

The nurse completes a nursing assessment of each ECC resident every month, records the findings and recommendations in the resident record, and reports changes in condition to the resident's health care provider and the Administrator (HCS-04).

The Administrator or ECC supervisor reviews each ECC resident's service plan every quarter with the nurse, the resident and the representative, and updates it. The review is signed and dated (ADM-03).

The Administrator sets the staffing schedule so that adequate awake staff are present at all hours to meet ECC residents' needs, in addition to meeting the staffing rules in Rule 59A-36.010 and STF-01. The written 24-hour staffing schedule is kept current.

If an ECC resident's needs exceed what the facility can safely provide, the Administrator acts under ADM-04 and ADM-05 and starts planning for relocation with the resident, representative and provider.

The Administrator keeps the ECC records required by Rule 59A-36.015, including ECC training records, nursing assessments, quarterly service plan reviews, and disclosures, at [ADDRESS] for AHCA inspection.

The Administrator reviews the ECC program every quarter: nursing assessment completion, service plan reviews, staffing adequacy, training status and resident outcomes, and reports the results to quality assurance (GOV-04).

If the ECC license lapses or is revoked, or the facility chooses to give it up, the Administrator notifies affected residents and representatives in writing, reassesses each ECC resident under ADM-02, and handles any needed discharge under ADM-05.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the ECC license, meets ECC experience and training requirements, ensures staffing, disclosure and record keeping, and oversees the program.
Supervises ECC services and staff, coordinates quarterly service plan reviews and completes required training.
Completes monthly nursing assessments, advises on care, and reports changes in condition.
Provide ECC services per the service plan and complete 2 hours of ECC in-service training within 6 months of hire.
Participate in service planning and quarterly reviews and acknowledge the ECC disclosure.

documentation: Current ECC license, posted (GOV-02)
Administrator experience documentation and ECC training records
Staff ECC in-service training records
Nurse employment or contract and license verification
Signed ECC disclosure (criteria, added services and costs, location limits)
Monthly nursing assessments
Quarterly service plan reviews
Written 24-hour staffing schedule showing awake staff
Quarterly ECC program review and QA records

policies.title: Limited Mental Health (LMH) Program
policies.applies_to: Administrator, managers and all staff with direct contact with mental health residents. This policy applies only while [AGENCY NAME] holds a Limited Mental Health (LMH) license from AHCA.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits and serves residents with a mental illness only under a valid LMH license, that each mental health resident has a community living support plan and a cooperative agreement on file, and that the Administrator, managers and direct-contact staff complete the specialized mental health training Florida requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not admit any mental health resident unless the facility license carries the LMH designation. For each mental health resident we keep a community living support plan and a cooperative agreement in the resident record. The Administrator, managers and every staff member with direct contact with mental health residents must complete 6 hours of specialized mental health training provided or approved by the Florida Department of Children and Families (DCF) within 6 months of the facility's LMH licensure or the person's employment, whichever applies. They then complete 3 hours of continuing education (CE) every 2 years. Training certificates are kept in the personnel file. The LMH designation carries no additional AHCA license fee.

definitions.definition: A specialty designation on the ALF license issued by AHCA under s. 429.075, F.S. It allows the facility to serve residents with a mental illness and requires specific staff training and resident-level documentation.
A resident with a diagnosed mental illness whom the facility serves under its LMH license, as defined by Florida law and AHCA.
The written plan for a mental health resident's living arrangements and supports in the facility. It is kept in the resident record.
The written agreement between the facility and the resident's community mental health provider describing how each will coordinate the resident's services. It is kept in the resident record.
Florida's mental health crisis law governing voluntary and involuntary examination. Staff are trained on its procedures as part of LMH continuing education.

procedures: Before any admission of a person with a mental illness, the Administrator confirms that the current AHCA license displays the LMH designation. If it does not, the person is not admitted as a mental health resident and the Administrator follows ADM-01 and ADM-04.

During pre-admission screening under ADM-01, the admissions staff member records whether the applicant has a diagnosed mental illness, the name of the community mental health provider, and current mental health medications and services. The Administrator reviews this before accepting the applicant.

For each mental health resident, the Administrator obtains the community living support plan and the cooperative agreement. They are completed with the resident, the resident's community mental health provider and, where applicable, the resident's representative.

The Administrator files both documents in the resident record and lists them on the admission checklist. A mental health resident's record is not considered complete until both are on file. The Administrator reviews missing items weekly until they are resolved.

Within 6 months of LMH licensure or of the person's start date, whichever applies, the Administrator, each manager and each staff member with direct contact with mental health residents completes 6 hours of specialized mental health training provided or approved by DCF.

The Administrator keeps an LMH training tracker showing each person's start date, due date, course provider, hours and completion date. The tracker is reviewed monthly. A staff member who has not completed the training is not assigned alone to the care of mental health residents without Administrator approval, and is scheduled for the next available course.

Every 2 years after the initial training, the same persons complete 3 hours of CE. Topics include: mental health diagnoses; mental health needs, services and behaviors; resident progress in treatment; recognizing changes in condition; and crisis services and Baker Act procedures.

For the Administrator and managers, the Administrator applies the initial 6 hours once toward 6 of their 12 hours of required CE, and counts the 3 hours of LMH CE toward the 12-hour requirement. The Administrator records this on the CE log.

When a new hire presents an LMH training certificate from a prior employer, the Administrator verifies that it is for DCF-provided or DCF-approved training and checks that it is complete. A copy is placed in the personnel file. The hours then count toward the new employer's requirement.

Staff observe and document the behaviors, mood, medication adherence and participation in services of each mental health resident. They report any change in condition to the Administrator or the shift lead the same shift, following HCS-04.

The Administrator notifies the resident's community mental health provider of significant changes and requests the provider's input on adjusting the community living support plan. The Administrator documents the contact in the resident record under ADM-03.

In a mental health crisis, staff stay with the resident, keep the environment safe and call the Administrator or on-call manager. If anyone is in imminent danger, staff call 911. Staff use Baker Act procedures as taught in training and do not use restraint except as allowed under SAF-04.

The Administrator coordinates with the resident's community mental health provider on the resident's progress in treatment at least as often as the cooperative agreement provides. The Administrator summarizes this in the record.
Mental health information is kept confidential under RR-07 and shared only as permitted by law and the resident's authorization. Medications are managed under HCS-01 and HCS-02.
The Administrator includes LMH records (plans, agreements, training completion) in the quality review under GOV-04 at least annually and corrects any gaps within 30 days.
LMH records are kept at the facility address and available to AHCA surveyors, and are retained under the time frames in the records policy.

responsibilities.duty: Decides to hold the LMH license, ensures resources for required training, and ensures no mental health resident is admitted without the license.

Verifies the LMH license before admission, obtains and files the community living support plan and cooperative agreement, schedules and tracks training, and maintains coordination with community mental health providers.
Complete required LMH training, supervise direct-contact staff on mental health resident care and report changes in condition.
Complete LMH training, observe and report behavior and condition changes, follow each resident's plan and respond to crises as trained.
Files each LMH training certificate and updates the training tracker.

documentation: AHCA license showing the LMH designation
Community living support plan for each mental health resident
Cooperative agreement for each mental health resident
LMH training tracker
LMH training certificates in each personnel file, including certificates from prior employers
CE log for the Administrator and managers
Resident record entries on changes in condition and contacts with the mental health provider
Annual LMH records review under GOV-04

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted staff, volunteers, the Administrator and the governing body
policies.purpose: To protect residents from abuse, neglect and exploitation, to ensure every suspected incident is reported to the Florida Abuse Hotline immediately, and to document prevention, training and response.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect and exploitation of residents. Every staff member must report any suspicion immediately to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 (1-800-96-ABUSE). Reporting to the Administrator does not replace reporting to the Hotline and must never delay it. No one will be retaliated against for a good-faith report. The Hotline number is posted in at least 14-point type near a telephone accessible to residents. Staff are screened with Level 2 background checks before working with residents and are trained on abuse prevention within 30 days of hire. Residents are never required to work without compensation, and staff do not serve as a resident's attorney in fact unless Florida law's conditions are met.

definitions.definition: Any willful act or threatened act that causes or is likely to cause significant impairment to a resident's physical, mental or emotional health, including hitting, restraining, verbal or emotional abuse, and sexual abuse.
Failure or omission to provide the care, supervision, food, medication or services necessary to maintain a resident's physical and mental health.
Improper use of a resident's funds, property or assets for the benefit of someone other than the resident, including through undue influence or coercion.
The DCF central abuse reporting line, 1-800-962-2873 (1-800-96-ABUSE), which receives reports of suspected abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults.
A fingerprint-based criminal background check required before staff and contracted staff work with residents. See STF-03.

procedures: The Administrator posts the Florida Abuse Hotline number, 1-800-962-2873 (1-800-96-ABUSE), in at least 14-point type near a telephone accessible to residents. The Administrator checks the posting monthly and records the check on the facility inspection log.
Before any employee or contracted staff member has contact with residents, the Administrator confirms completion of Level 2 screening under STF-03 and files the result in the personnel file.

New direct care staff who have not completed core training receive 1 hour of training within 30 days of hire on resident rights and on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation. The training uses this policy and the facility's abuse prevention procedures. The trainer records the date, hours and trainee signature.
At hire, each employee signs an acknowledgement that they have received this policy and understand that they must report immediately to the Hotline. The signed form is kept in the personnel file.

Any person who sees, hears of or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation of a resident must immediately stop any ongoing harm, ensure the resident is safe and call the Florida Abuse Hotline. If a resident needs medical care or is in immediate danger, staff call 911 first.

The reporting staff member then informs the Administrator or on-call manager. If the Administrator is the person suspected, the staff member informs the governing body representative. The facility does not require staff to obtain permission before reporting to the Hotline.

The Administrator or manager separates the resident from the alleged perpetrator. If the alleged perpetrator is an employee, they are removed from resident contact pending the outcome of the investigation.
The Administrator arranges medical evaluation of the resident if needed and notifies the resident's representative, family and physician as appropriate, unless the person is the alleged perpetrator.

The reporting staff member and the Administrator complete an incident report under SAF-02 the same shift. The report records who, what, when, where, witnesses, the Hotline call date, time and confirmation number, and actions taken. Staff preserve evidence and do not alter the scene.
The facility cooperates fully with DCF, law enforcement, AHCA and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman. See RR-03.

The Administrator conducts an internal review within 72 hours of the report, without interfering with the official investigation, and takes corrective action. Where substantiated, the corrective action includes discipline up to termination.
Residents are not required to perform work without compensation. Any resident who chooses to do tasks does so voluntarily, with a written arrangement and fair compensation.

Staff do not act as a resident's attorney in fact unless Florida law's conditions, including the required monthly statement to the resident and the required surety bond, are met. The Administrator reviews any such request before it is accepted and documents the review.
The house rules given to residents include a statement on reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation. The Administrator reviews the house rules annually.
The Administrator reviews all abuse-related reports and trends in the quality review under GOV-04 at least quarterly, and keeps this policy on file at the facility.

responsibilities.duty: Immediately report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the Hotline, protect the resident and inform the Administrator.
Ensures posting, background screening and training, protects the resident, completes the incident report and internal review, and cooperates with investigators.
Receives reports involving the Administrator, and ensures that no retaliation occurs.
Delivers and documents the 1-hour training within 30 days of hire.

documentation: Photo or inspection log entry showing the Hotline posting
Written abuse prevention policies and procedures on file
Training sign-in sheets and records of the 1-hour training
Signed employee acknowledgement in the personnel file
Level 2 screening results
Incident reports with Hotline call date, time and confirmation number
Internal review notes and corrective action
Notification records to the resident's representative and physician
Documentation of any attorney-in-fact arrangement, monthly statements and surety bond

policies.title: Incident and Accident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator and managers
policies.purpose: To ensure every incident, accident, injury, medication error and significant change in a resident is promptly addressed, documented, reported to the right parties and reviewed to prevent recurrence.
policies.policy: All incidents and accidents involving residents, staff or visitors are reported to the Administrator or manager on duty immediately and documented in writing before the end of the shift. Significant changes in a resident and illnesses resulting in medical attention are recorded in the resident record. Medication errors, refusals and missed doses are recorded on the medication observation record. The Administrator reports adverse incidents to AHCA, and carries out risk management duties, in the form and within the time required by Florida law. Evacuations are reported to the county emergency management agency and AHCA within 6 hours of the evacuation order.

definitions.definition: Any unusual or unexpected event involving a resident, such as a fall, injury, elopement, altercation, medication error, or suspected abuse.
An incident that meets the definition used by Florida law and AHCA for reportable adverse incidents. The Administrator applies the current AHCA definition.
A change in a resident's physical or mental condition that requires medical attention or a change in services or care.
The record on which staff document each resident's medication assistance, including errors, refusals and missed doses.

procedures: Within 30 days of hire, direct care staff receive 1 hour of in-service training on reporting adverse incidents and on the facility's emergency procedures, including chain of command and staff roles in evacuation. The trainer records the date, hours and trainee signature.

When an incident or accident occurs, the nearest staff member first ensures resident safety and summons emergency help (911) if needed, then notifies the manager on duty or the Administrator at [PHONE] immediately.
The manager on duty assesses the resident, provides first aid within staff training and the facility's scope, and, when indicated, follows HCS-04 for physician notification and hospital transfer.

The staff member who witnessed or discovered the incident completes an incident report before the end of the shift. It records the resident, date, time, location, a factual description, witnesses, injuries, immediate actions, who was notified and when.

The manager on duty notifies the resident's representative or family, and the physician or health care provider as appropriate, and documents the time and person contacted. If the incident involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, staff also follow SAF-01 immediately.
A significant change in a resident, and any illness resulting in medical attention, is recorded in the resident record the same shift, under ADM-03.
Medication errors, refusals and missed doses are recorded on the MOR the moment they are identified. Staff notify the Administrator or nurse, and the prescriber when needed, following HCS-02.

The Administrator reviews every incident report within 1 business day, determines whether it is an adverse incident reportable to AHCA, and, if so, submits the report to AHCA in the form and within the time required by Florida law. The Administrator reviews the current AHCA requirements at least annually and whenever AHCA announces changes.
The Administrator performs risk management for adverse incidents, including investigation, a review of contributing factors and corrective action, and documents that work.

When a county evacuation order is issued under SAF-05, the Administrator notifies the county emergency management agency and AHCA within 6 hours of the order and documents the date, time and person contacted.

Incident reports are filed in an incident log kept at the facility and a copy is placed in the resident's record when it concerns that resident. Records are retained under the facility's records schedule.
The Administrator updates the resident's care plan or service plan under ADM-03 when an incident shows a need for changed care, such as after a fall.
Each month the Administrator tabulates incidents by type, time, location and resident, and presents the trends to the quality committee under GOV-04.
Where an incident reveals a training gap, the Administrator schedules retraining within 30 days and records it.

responsibilities.duty: Protect the resident, report immediately and complete an accurate incident report before shift end.
Assess, notify the physician and family, ensure documentation and notify the Administrator.
Reviews incidents, makes AHCA adverse incident reports, performs risk management, reports evacuations and leads trend analysis.
Reviews monthly incident trends and recommends corrective action under GOV-04.

Resident record entries on significant changes and illnesses requiring medical attention
Medication observation records documenting errors, refusals and missed doses
AHCA adverse incident reports and confirmations

policies.title: Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator and managers
policies.purpose: To identify residents at risk of elopement, prevent residents from leaving the facility unsafely and unsupervised, and respond immediately and effectively when a resident is missing.
policies.policy: All residents are assessed for elopement risk within 30 days of admission. Residents assessed at risk, or with any history of elopement, are identified to staff. A missing resident triggers an immediate search of the facility and premises under defined staff duties, followed by contact with law enforcement, family, guardian, health care surrogate and case manager if the resident is not found. The care of all other residents continues without interruption. Elopement drills are conducted and documented. All staff are trained within 30 days of employment, receive a copy of this policy and demonstrate competency.

definitions.definition: A resident leaving the facility or its grounds without the knowledge or supervision needed for the resident's safety.
A resident assessed as at risk of elopement, or one with any history of elopement.
A practice exercise of the missing-resident response, documented with participants and outcome.

procedures: During pre-admission screening under ADM-01, staff ask about any history of elopement, wandering or exit-seeking and record the answer. The Administrator reviews it before approving admission.

Within 30 days of admission, and after any significant change, the Administrator or a designated manager assesses the elopement risk of each resident and documents the result in the resident record under ADM-02.

The Administrator maintains a list of at-risk residents and residents with a history of elopement. The list is available to every shift, and staff are told of any new addition at or before the next shift change.
Each day, staff make an effort to check that each at-risk resident carries ID with the resident's name and the facility's name, address and phone [ADDRESS] [PHONE]. Staff document the daily check.
The facility keeps a current photo ID for each at-risk resident, kept in an area accessible to staff and available to law enforcement.

When a resident is discovered or suspected missing, the first staff member to notice calls out to the manager on duty immediately and begins searching the area. Staff may not wait to confirm before starting.

The manager on duty becomes the search leader. The leader assigns staff to search each area of the building and the grounds, including exits, stairwells, bathrooms, vehicles, nearby streets and water, and records the time started.
The leader assigns one staff member to keep caring for the other residents, and ensures no resident is left unsupervised and that supervision is maintained.

If the resident is not found within the time in the facility's search plan, or at once if the resident is high risk or conditions are unsafe, the leader calls 911 and gives law enforcement the resident's description, photo, clothing, medical conditions and last known location.
The leader or designee then contacts the resident's family, guardian, health care surrogate and case manager, and the Administrator at [PHONE], and documents the time and person contacted for each.
When the resident is found, staff check for injury, notify the physician as needed under HCS-04, tell law enforcement and others, and document the time and condition.

The staff members complete an incident report under SAF-02 the same shift. The Administrator reviews how the resident left, repairs any gap, reassesses the resident's risk and updates the service plan under ADM-03.

The Administrator conducts and documents elopement drills at the frequency required by Florida law. The log shows the date, time, scenario, participants and result. Direct care staff and the Administrator participate, and their participation is recorded in the personnel file.

Within 30 days of employment, each staff member is trained on this policy, receives a copy of it and shows competency, for example through a drill or a skills check. The trainer documents the training and files it in the personnel file.
The elopement policy is included in the admission package given under ADM-01, and the house rules reflect it. The Administrator keeps documentation of elopement drills at the facility.

responsibilities.duty: Know the at-risk residents, search immediately and follow assigned duties.
Leads the search, calls law enforcement, notifies family, guardian, health care surrogate and case manager, and keeps care of other residents going.
Ensures risk assessments, the at-risk list, photo IDs, drills, training and corrective action.
Keep care of the remaining residents during a search.

documentation: Elopement risk assessment in each resident record
At-risk resident list and daily ID check log
Photo ID file
Incident reports and search timeline
Notification log for law enforcement, family, guardian, surrogate and case manager
Elopement drill records
Personnel file documentation of staff and Administrator drill participation
Staff training and competency records with policy acknowledgement
Admission package acknowledgement and house rules

policies.title: Physical and Chemical Restraints and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: Administrator, managers, nursing and direct care staff, and the resident's physician
policies.purpose: To make sure restraints are used only with a physician's prescription and a written care plan, applied safely, monitored and reviewed, and that restrictive practices are not used for convenience or discipline.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not use physical restraints for staff convenience or as discipline. A physical restraint may be used only with a physician's prescription and a written care plan that is in place before use and completed within 14 days of the prescription. The physician reviews the continued need at least annually. A device a resident can sometimes remove or avoid and sometimes cannot is treated as a physical restraint. A medication that serves as a chemical restraint requires a record of the prescribing physician's annual evaluation. Staff must apply any device appropriately and safely.

definitions.definition: Any device or method that restricts a resident's freedom of movement or normal access to the body. This includes a device the resident cannot reliably remove or avoid.
A medication used to control a resident's behavior or restrict movement, rather than to treat a medical or psychiatric condition.
A written plan stating the device, the maximum time per day it will be applied, and how and how often staff will monitor the resident and report problems to the physician.
A resident's ability to remove or avoid a device changes, so that at times the resident cannot. In that situation the device is treated as a restraint.

procedures: Staff may not apply any physical restraint without a written physician prescription. The Administrator verifies that the prescription is in the resident record before the first use.

Before considering a restraint, the Administrator and nurse or care manager review less restrictive alternatives, such as environmental changes, toileting, pain assessment, activities, additional supervision and, for falls, HCS-06 measures. The review is documented.

The Administrator or designee, with the physician's input, writes a restraint care plan before the device is first used, and in all cases within 14 days of the prescription. The plan states the device, the maximum number of hours per day it may be applied, and how and how often staff monitor the resident.
The plan requires staff to report to the physician any injury, agitation, depression or decline in mobility linked to the device. The plan states the staff member to notify and the timeframe.
Staff are trained on the specific device, and only trained staff apply it. The device is applied as prescribed, appropriately and safely, and the resident is not left in distress.

Staff monitor the resident at the frequency in the care plan and record each check, time applied, time removed and any injury, agitation or change. They report problems to the Administrator and physician immediately.
If a resident's ability to remove or avoid a device varies, the Administrator treats the device as a restraint and follows steps 1 through 6 before it continues to be used.

The physician reviews the continued appropriateness of the restraint at least annually. The Administrator tracks due dates and files each review in the resident record. If the physician does not review it in time, use is stopped and the Administrator contacts the physician.
The Administrator reassesses at each reassessment under ADM-02 and after any change of condition whether the restraint is still needed, and updates the care plan.

For medications that act as chemical restraints, the Administrator confirms that a record of the prescribing physician's evaluation is in the resident record every year. Staff do not ask for or give medication for the purpose of controlling behavior for staff convenience.

Staff administer or assist with medications only under HCS-01 and HCS-02. Staff report to the physician and the Administrator any resident who shows sedation, falls or behavior change after a medication change.
Staff do not use restraints in an emergency to hold a resident without a prescription. In imminent danger, they call 911 and follow HCS-04 and, for mental health crises, HCS-12.
Secured units and locked areas are governed by HCS-05 and are not substituted for a restraint plan.
Bed rails and other assistive devices are governed by HCS-10. If a device would restrict a resident's movement against the resident's will, this policy applies.

The facility's physical restraint policy is kept on file at the facility, and the house rules include it. The Administrator reviews both at least annually and reports restraint use in the quality review under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Prescribes any restraint, helps develop the care plan, reviews appropriateness at least annually, and evaluates chemical restraint medications annually.
Verifies the prescription and care plan, tracks annual reviews, trains staff, and ensures alternatives are tried and use is monitored.
Apply devices safely and as prescribed, monitor the resident, document each check and report problems.
Assesses the resident, helps write the care plan and monitors for harm.

documentation: Physician's prescription for each physical restraint
Written restraint care plan with device, maximum daily time and monitoring plan
Restraint monitoring log
Documentation of alternatives considered
Physician's annual review of continued appropriateness
Record of the physician's annual evaluation for medications used as chemical restraints
Reports to the physician of injury, agitation, depression or decline in mobility
Staff training records on devices
Restraint policy on file and house rules

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan
policies.applies_to: Administrator, managers and all staff
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] has a written Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan (CEMP) approved by the county, that staff are trained on it, and that residents are protected, evacuated and accounted for during and after a disaster.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written CEMP on AHCA Form 3180-5006, "Minimum Emergency Management Planning Criteria for Assisted Living Facilities" (Sept 2023). It covers all hazards. The plan is reviewed and submitted every year to the county emergency management agency, which has final authority over it. Significant modifications are submitted within 30 days. All staff are trained on their duties, and new staff within 30 days of hire. If directed by the county, the facility evacuates and reports the evacuation to the county and AHCA within 6 hours of the order.

definitions.definition: The facility's written plan for preparing for, responding to and recovering from emergencies, completed on AHCA Form 3180-5006.
A major change to the plan, such as to the facility's evacuation destination, transportation, contacts or capacity, which must be submitted to the county within 30 days.
Moving residents out of the facility at the direction of the county, or on the facility's own decision when life safety requires it.
Housing people in the facility above its licensed capacity during a declared state of emergency, allowed only if life safety is not jeopardized and needs can be met.

procedures: The Administrator writes and keeps the CEMP on AHCA Form 3180-5006 (Sept 2023). It covers all hazards, and the care of residents who stay, in the facility and those who are evacuated, including records, transportation, sheltering, supplies, staffing, equipment and medications.

The CEMP also addresses care of evacuees the facility receives, residents with Alzheimer's disease and related disorders or mobility limits, coordination with the county, and post-disaster activities, including answering family inquiries and reporting relocations to the county. It names the staff responsible for each part.

Each year, the Administrator reviews the plan and submits it to the county emergency management agency for approval. The Administrator follows the county's directions on changes, since the county has final authority over the plan.
If the plan is significantly modified during the year, the Administrator submits the change to the county within 30 days and records the date submitted.
The Administrator keeps the approved plan, with documentation of county approval, at the facility where it is readily available to staff and surveyors.
The Administrator trains all staff on their duties under the plan. New staff are trained within 30 days of hire, and the trainer records the date, topics and trainee signature in the personnel file.

The Administrator keeps a 3-day supply of nonperishable food and water, or a water plan reviewed by the local disaster preparedness authority. Checks are made monthly, and in the start of each hurricane season, with stock rotated and recorded.

The Administrator keeps a current resident roster with medications, diagnoses, mobility needs, contacts and any ADRD status, ready to travel with residents on evacuation. The roster is updated at least monthly and when a resident is admitted or discharged.

When a storm or other threat is forecast, the Administrator activates the plan, checks supplies, medications, vehicles and generators under SAF-06, calls staff in and tells residents' representatives of the plan.

If the county directs evacuation, the Administrator evacuates residents following the CEMP. The Administrator reports the evacuation to the county and AHCA within 6 hours of the order and records the time, the person told and the destination.

During evacuation, staff keep track of the location of every resident until each has been relocated. Staff document each resident's destination and transport, and send medications and records with the resident.
The Administrator keeps a contact person available to AHCA 24 hours a day, 7 days a week during the emergency, and gives AHCA the contact's name and number: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE].
If telephones fail, staff request help from law enforcement or emergency management by other means available under the CEMP.
The facility does not re-occupy until the county clears re-entry and the Administrator confirms that the facility can meet residents' needs.
